Option D (delete via REST API) — a record-at-a-time (or small composite) mechanism with no hard-delete operation; not built for millions of rows.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_deleting_data.htm

question: What makes Skinny tables fast? Choose three answers.
optionA: They do not include soft-deleted records
optionB: They avoid resource intensive joins
optionC: Their tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified
optionD: They can contain fields from other objects
optionE: They support up to a max of 100 of columns
explanation:
They do not include soft-deleted records, they avoid resource-intensive joins, and they are kept in sync with their source tables — the Skinny Tables page states all three. They "omit soft-deleted records". Salesforce "can create skinny tables to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins" — the join avoided is between the base table and the custom-field table. And "Skinny tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified", which is what makes them usable without a refresh step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option D (can contain fields from other objects) — the inverse of the documented rule: "Skinny tables can't contain fields from other objects."
Option E (up to 100 columns) — wrong on its number; the documented cap is "Skinny tables can contain a maximum of 200 columns".
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_skinny_tables.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation accepted option E's "100-column cap" as a real limit that merely wasn't a performance driver. The documented maximum is 200 columns, so E is false on its face, not just irrelevant.

question: DreamHouse Realty has a data model as shown in the image. The Project object has a private sharing model, and it has Roll-Up summary fields to calculate the number of resources assigned to the project, total hours for the project, and the number of work items associated to the project. There will be a large amount of time entry records to be loaded regularly from an external system into Salesforce. What should the Architect consider in this situation?
optionA: Load all data after deferring sharing calculations.
optionB: Calculate summary values instead of Roll-Up by using workflow.
optionC: Calculate summary values instead of Roll-Up by using triggers.
optionD: Load all data using external IDs to link to parent records.
explanation:
Loading all data after deferring sharing calculations is the consideration. The figure above is the model the stem refers to, and the cascade it shows is the whole problem: Time Entry is a junction with master-detail to both Work Item and Resource, each of which rolls its hours up, and those two are themselves master-detail children of Project, which rolls up again. So one Time Entry insert recalculates roll-ups on two parents and then on their shared grandparent — and Project is private, so its sharing is recalculated on top of that. Loading that feed regularly is exactly what the LDV guide's remedy is written for: "Use the defer sharing calculation permission to defer sharing calculations until after all data has been loaded", then run one recalculation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (workflow instead of roll-ups) — swaps a platform-maintained aggregate for automation that fires on every insert and walks the same two-level cascade by hand; more work per record, not less.
Option C (triggers instead of roll-ups) — the same trade, in code.
Option D (external IDs to link parents) — how you resolve the parent references during the load; it does nothing about the recalculation cost, which is what the stem asks about.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deferred_sharing_calculation.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: A large Automobile company has implemented SF for its Sales Associates. Leads flow from its website to SF using a batch integration in SF. The Batch job connects the leads to Accounts in SF. Customer visiting their retail stores are also created in SF as Accounts. The company has noticed a large number of duplicate accounts in SF. On analysis, it was found that certain customers could interact with its website and also visit the store. The Sales associates use Global Search to search for customers in Salesforce before they create the customers. Which scalable option should a data Architect choose to implement to avoid duplicates?
optionA: Create duplicate rules in SF to validate duplicates during the account creation process
optionB: Implement a MDM solution to validate the customer information before creating Accounts in SF.
optionC: Build Custom search based on fields on Accounts which can be matched with customer when they visit the store
optionD: Customize Account creation process to search if customer exists before creating an Account.
explanation:
Creating duplicate rules in Salesforce to validate duplicates during account creation is the scalable option. Native Duplicate Management with matching and duplicate rules catches matches at both the batch-integration insert and the manual store-created insert without custom code — the low-maintenance choice that covers both entry paths.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an MDM solution) — heavier infrastructure than the problem needs; the duplicates arise inside one org at two insert points.
Option C (custom search on Account fields) — duplicates platform capability with development effort, and only helps the in-store path.
Option D (customise account creation to search first) — the same custom-code route, and it does not cover the batch integration.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is migrating data from legacy system to Salesforce. During data analysis it was discovered that data types of fields being migrated do not match with Salesforce data types. Which solution should a data architect use to ensure successful data migrations?
optionA: Migrate legacy data to a staging database for mapping then leverage an ETL tool to transform the data and load into Salesforce.
optionB: Export legacy data into the staging database and leverage stored procedures to transform data types before loading into Salesforce.
optionC: Migrate the legacy data leveraging an ETL tool to transform data types and load data into Salesforce.
optionD: Export legacy data into CSV files and leverage data loader to load data into Salesforce.
explanation:
Migrating the legacy data with an ETL tool that transforms the data types and loads into Salesforce is the solution. An ETL tool transforms mismatched data types in flight — that is the T in ETL — so it maps legacy types to Salesforce types, cleanses, and loads in one pipeline.
This is a tooling-judgment item: Salesforce documents the load mechanisms rather than ranking ETL against a staging database for this scenario.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (staging database for mapping, then ETL) — stands up infrastructure to do work the ETL layer already does.
Option B (staging database with stored procedures) — the same extra infrastructure, with the transformation hand-written.
Option D (CSV files and Data Loader) — Data Loader reads a CSV and writes it; it performs no type transformation, so a mismatched source simply fails on load.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Northern trail Outfitters (NTO) uses Sales Cloud and service Cloud to manage sales and support processes. Some of NTOs team are complaining they see new fields on their page unsure of which values need be input. NTO is concerned about lack of governance in making changes to Salesforce. Which governance measure should a data architect recommend to solve this issue?
optionA: Add description fields to explain why the field is used, and mark the field as required.
optionB: Create and manage a data dictionary and set up a governance process for changes made to common objects.
optionC: Create reports to identify which users are leaving fields blank, and use external data sources to augment the missing data.
optionD: Create validation rules with error messages to explain why the fields is used
explanation:
Creating and managing a data dictionary and setting up a governance process for changes to common objects is the measure. A maintained data dictionary documents each field's purpose, and a change-governance process controls who can add fields and why — addressing the root cause of uncontrolled, undocumented metadata changes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (description fields and mark required) — treats the symptom on individual fields and does not govern who adds the next one; marking fields required is a separate decision the stem never asks for.
Option C (reports on blank fields, external data to fill them) — measures the problem rather than preventing it.
Option D (validation rules with explanatory errors) — explains a field at save time, one field at a time, with no governance of change.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) owns a complex Salesforce org with many Apex classes, triggers, and automated processes that will modify records if available. UC has identified that, in its current development state, UC runs change of encountering race condition on the same record. What should a data architect recommend to guarantee that records are not being updated at the same time?
optionA: Embed the keywords FOR UPDATE after SOQL statements.
optionB: Disable classes or triggers that have the potential to obtain the same record.
optionC: Migrate programmatic logic to processes and flows.
optionD: Refactor or optimize classes and trigger for maximum CPU performance.
explanation:
Embedding FOR UPDATE after the SOQL statements is the recommendation. FOR UPDATE takes a row lock on the selected records for the duration of the transaction, so a competing transaction must wait — which prevents the lost-update race condition.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (disable classes or triggers) — removes functionality rather than coordinating concurrency.
Option C (move logic to processes and flows) — provides no pessimistic locking; flows race just as Apex does.
Option D (optimise for CPU performance) — addresses governor limits, not concurrency.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_locking_records.htm

question: UC has a legacy client server app that as a relational data base that needs to be migrated to Salesforce. What are the 3 key actions that should be done when data modeling in Salesforce? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Identify data elements to be persisted in Salesforce.
optionB: Map legacy data to Salesforce objects.
optionC: Map legacy data to Salesforce custom objects.
optionD: Work with legacy application owner to analysis legacy data model.
optionE: Implement legacy data model within Salesforce using custom fields.
explanation:
Identifying the data elements to be persisted in Salesforce, mapping legacy data to Salesforce objects, and implementing the model with custom fields are the three keyed actions. Migrating a relational schema starts by deciding what actually needs to live in Salesforce rather than porting the whole database, mapping the elements that survive onto Salesforce objects, and then realising that model with custom objects and fields.
Be aware this item is loose: option D, analysing the legacy model with its application owner, is at least as defensible a third choice as E, and the two are not mutually exclusive. Treat A and B as the solid pair and the third slot as the item's weak point.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (map legacy data to custom objects) — a strict subset of B: mapping to custom objects is one outcome of mapping to objects, since much of a legacy model lands on standard objects such as Account, Contact and Opportunity.
Option D (analyse the legacy model with its owner) — a sound step, and the item's weak point; it is not keyed only because the exam's three are A, B and E.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: option C is a strict subset of keyed option B, and distractor D (analyse the legacy data model with its owner) is at least as defensible as keyed option E. The key is the exam's, but the third choice is not decidable from the stem.

question: UC has millions of Cases and are running out of storage. Some user groups need to have access to historical cases for up to 7 years. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommend in order to minimize performance and storage issues? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Export data out of Salesforce and store in Flat files on external system.
optionB: Create a custom object to store case history and run reports on it.
optionC: Leverage on premise data archival and build integration to view archived data.
optionD: Leverage big object to archive case data and lightning components to show archived data.
explanation:
On-premise data archival with an integration to view the archived data, and big objects with Lightning components to show archived cases, are the two solutions. Both move volume off the transactional store while keeping 7-year data accessible to the user groups that need it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (export to flat files on an external system) — makes the data hard to query and gives users no way to view it from Salesforce.
Option B (a custom object for case history) — still consumes storage and degrades performance at millions of rows; it moves the problem sideways.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has three systems: Salesforce, a cloud-based ERP system, and an on-premise Order Management System (OMS). An architect has been tasked with creating a solution that uses Salesforce as the system of record for Leads and the OMS as the system of record for Account and Contacts. UC wants Accounts and Contacts to be able to maintain their names in each system (i.e., "John Doe" in the OMS and "Johnny Doe" in Salesforce), but wants to have a consolidated data store which links referenced records across the systems. What approach should an architect suggest so the requirements are met?
optionA: Have Salesforce poll the OMS nightly and bring in the desired Accounts and Contacts.
optionB: Implement an integration tool to send OMS Accounts and Contacts to Salesforce.
optionC: Implement a Master Data Management strategy to reconcile Leads, Accounts, and Contacts.
optionD: Use the Streaming API to send Account and Contact data from Salesforce to the OMS.
explanation:
Implementing a Master Data Management strategy to reconcile Leads, Accounts and Contacts is the approach. Three things in this stem only MDM delivers together: a different system of record per entity (Salesforce for Leads, the OMS for Accounts and Contacts), deliberate attribute divergence ("John Doe" in one system and "Johnny Doe" in the other), and a consolidated store that cross-references the same real customer across systems.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer to this scenario.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce polls the OMS nightly) — point-to-point sync: whichever side writes last flattens the other's name, and it produces no cross-reference store.
Option B (integration tool sending OMS Accounts and Contacts to Salesforce) — the same one-way copy; it overwrites the divergent names the requirement wants kept.
Option D (Streaming API from Salesforce to the OMS) — delivers event messages one way; it reconciles nothing.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers has millions of rows of data in Salesforce that are being used in reports to evaluate historical trends. Performance has become an issue, as well as data storage limits. Which two strategies should be recommended when talking with stakeholders?
optionA: Use scheduled batch Apex to copy aggregate information into a custom object and delete the original records.
optionB: Combine Analytics Snapshots with a purging plan by reporting on the snapshot data and deleting the original records.
optionC: Use Data Loader to extract data, aggregate it, and write it back to a custom object, then delete the original records.
optionD: Configure the Salesforce Archiving feature to archive older records and remove them from the data storage limits.
explanation:
Scheduled batch Apex that copies aggregate information into a custom object and deletes the originals, and Analytics Snapshots combined with a purging plan, are the two strategies. Reporting Snapshots are the native mechanism for exactly this problem: they "let you report on historical data" by saving "tabular or summary report results to fields on a custom object" on a schedule — snapshot the trend data, then purge the detail rows behind it. Scheduled batch Apex that rolls detail into a summary object and deletes the originals reaches the same place under your own control.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Data Loader to extract, aggregate and write back) — Data Loader extracts and loads; it does not aggregate, so that round trip cannot produce the summary the stem needs.
Option D (Salesforce Archiving feature) — not the empty distractor it once was: Salesforce Archive is a real, separately purchased product whose policies "regularly offload inactive records, files, and attachments from production". It is not keyed because it addresses only storage and does nothing for the historical trend reporting that is the other half of the requirement.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.data_about_analytic_snap.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/data-archiving-solutions/

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option D on the ground that "there is no general native 'Salesforce Archiving feature'" — an invented absence. Salesforce Archive exists as a purchasable product with automated archiving policies that remove records from production.

question: UC is building a Salesforce application to track contacts and their respective conferences that they have attended with the following requirements: 1.Contacts will be stored in the standard contact object. 2.Conferences will be stored in a custom conference_ c object. 3.Each contact may attend multiple conferences and each conference may be related to multiple contacts. How should a data architect model the relationship between the contact and conference objects?
optionA: Implement a Contact Conference junction object with master detail relationship to both contact and Conference__c
optionB: Create a master detail relationship field on the Contact object.
optionC: Create a master detail relationship field on the Conference object.
optionD: Create a lookup relationship field on contact object.
explanation:
A Contact Conference junction object with master-detail relationships to both Contact and Conference__c is the model. A many-to-many relationship requires a junction object with two master-detail relationships, letting each contact attend many conferences and each conference include many contacts while enforcing referential integrity.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (master-detail on Contact) — a single relationship models one-to-many only, and Contact cannot be made the detail of a custom object.
Option C (master-detail on Conference) — one-to-many again: each conference would relate to one contact.
Option D (lookup on Contact) — one-to-many, and without the junction there is nowhere to record each attendance.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a business that works directly with individual consumers (B2C). They are moving from a current home-grown CRM system to Salesforce. UC has about one million consumer records. What should the architect recommend for optimal use of Salesforce functionality and also to avoid data loading issues?
optionA: Create a Custom Object Individual_Consumer__c to load all individual consumers.
optionB: Load all individual consumers as Account records and avoid using the Contact object.
optionC: Load one Account record and one Contact record for each individual consumer.
optionD: Create one Account and load individual consumers as Contacts linked to that one Account.
explanation:
One Account record and one Contact record for each individual consumer is the recommendation. It is the standard business-account B2C model when Person Accounts are not on the table — the same shape Person Accounts create internally. No parent carries more than one child, so there is no skew and no load contention, and both standard objects keep their full functionality.
Salesforce names option D's design as an anti-pattern by its own worked example. Parent-Child Data Skew describes skew as "a large number of child records (10,000 or more)" on one parent, and illustrates it with "a customer with hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account" — which is precisely what loading a million consumers as Contacts under a single Account produces. Even the LDV guide's bucket-account workaround says to "set up several dummy accounts and distribute the contacts among them", never one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom Individual_Consumer__c object) — throws away everything that works on Contact: activities, campaign members, cases, duplicate rules.
Option B (consumers as Accounts with no Contacts) — leaves nothing to attach activities, campaign members or cases to.
Option D (one Account with a million Contacts) — the documented parent-child skew anti-pattern; every insert contends for the same parent row and the design fails the stem's own "avoid data loading issues" test.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

corrected.note: Key moved D to C. The deck keyed the single-bucket-account pattern, which is the exact configuration Salesforce's Parent-Child Data Skew page uses as its example of what not to do ("hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account"), and which causes the load contention the stem asks to avoid. The LDV guide's own bucket workaround specifies several dummy accounts, not one.

question:
Universal Containers (UC) is in the process of selling half of its company. As part of this split, UC's main Salesforce org will be divided into two org: org A and org B. UC has delivered these requirements to its data architect:
1. The data model for Org B will drastically change with different objects, fields, and picklist values.
2. Three million records will need to be migrated from org A to org B for compliance reasons.
3. The migrate will need occur within the next two month, prior to be split.
Which migrate strategy should a data architect use to successfully migrate the date?
optionA: use as ETL tool to orchestrate the migration.
optionB: Use Data Loader for export and Data Import Wizard for import
optionC: Write a script to use the Bulk API
optionD: Use the Salesforce CLI to query, export, and import
explanation:
Using an ETL tool to orchestrate the migration is the strategy. The distinguishing requirement is transformation, not volume: Org B has different objects, fields and picklist values, so every record has to be remapped in flight. An ETL tool is built for that — extract, transform against the new model, load — and can be re-run repeatedly as the mapping is refined across a two-month window.
This is a tooling-judgment item — Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than ranking them for an org split.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data Loader export, Data Import Wizard import) — the Import Wizard is limited to a small set of objects and record counts and performs no transformation.
Option C (a script against the Bulk API) — can move three million records, but you would be building the mapping, value translation and error handling the ETL layer already provides.
Option D (Salesforce CLI to query, export and import) — the same: a transport with no transformation layer.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Get Cloudy Consulting uses an invoicing system that has specific requirements. One requirement is that attachments associated with the Invoice__c custom object be classified by Types (i.e., "Purchase Order", "Receipt", etc.) so that reporting can be performed on invoices showing the number of attachments grouped by Type. What should an Architect do to categorize the attachments to fulfill these requirements?
optionA: Add additional options to the standard ContentType picklist field for the Attachment object.
optionB: Add a ContentType picklist field to the Attachment layout and create additional picklist options.
optionC: Create a custom picklist field for the Type on the standard Attachment object with the values.
optionD: Create a custom object related to the Invoice object with a picklist field for the Type.
explanation:
A custom object related to Invoice__c with a picklist field for the Type is what the architect should build. The classic Attachment object does not support custom fields, so the supported pattern is a related custom object that stores each attachment reference plus a Type picklist, which is what enables reporting grouped by Type.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (add values to a standard ContentType picklist on Attachment) — Attachment has no such picklist; ContentType is a read-only MIME-type field.
Option B (add a ContentType picklist to the Attachment layout) — the Attachment object does not accept custom fields, so there is nothing to add.
Option C (custom Type picklist on Attachment) — the same: custom fields cannot be created on the standard Attachment object.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has adopted Salesforce as its primary sales automated tool. UC has 100,00 customers with a growth rate of 10% a year, UC uses an on-premise web-based billing and invoice system that generates over 1 million invoices a year supporting a monthly billing cycle. The UC sales team needs to be able to pull a customer record and view their account status, Invoice history, and opportunities without navigating outside of Salesforce. What should a data architect use to provide the sales team with the required functionality?
optionA: Create a custom object and migrate the last 12 months of Invoice data into Salesforce so it can be displayed on the Account layout.
optionB: Write an Apex callout and populate a related list to display on the account record.
optionC: Create a mashup page that will present the billing system records within Salesforce.
optionD: Create a visual force tab with the billing system encapsulated within an iframe.
explanation:
A mashup page that presents the billing system's records within Salesforce is what the sales team needs. A mashup surfaces the high-volume billing and invoice data live from the on-premise system inside the customer record without copying a million-plus invoices a year into Salesforce, giving sales the consolidated view while avoiding storage cost and stale data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (migrate 12 months of invoices into a custom object) — consumes storage, goes stale between loads, and still leaves older history outside.
Option B (Apex callout populating a related list) — custom code for what a mashup or external object gives declaratively, and a related list implies records that exist in Salesforce.
Option D (Visualforce tab with the billing system in an iframe) — does not present the data in the context of the customer record the rep has pulled up.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_using_mashups.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses Salesforce for tracking opportunities (Opportunity). UC uses an internal ERP system for tracking deliveries and invoicing. The ERP system supports SOAP API and OData for bi-directional integration between Salesforce and the ERP system. UC has about one million opportunities. For each opportunity, UC sends 12 invoices, one per month. UC sales reps have requirements to view current invoice status and invoice amount from the opportunity page. When creating an object to model invoices, what should the architect recommend, considering performance and data storage space?
optionA: Use Streaming API to get the current status from the ERP and display on the Opportunity page.
optionB: Create an external object Invoice__x with a Lookup relationship with Opportunity.
optionC: Create a custom object Invoice__c with a master-detail relationship with Opportunity.
optionD: Create a custom object Invoice__c with a Lookup relationship with Opportunity.
explanation:
An external object Invoice__x with a lookup relationship to Opportunity is the recommendation. With 12 million invoices that live in the ERP and only need to be viewed, an external object via OData keeps the data off-platform — zero storage cost and always current — while still letting reps see status and amount on the Opportunity through an external or indirect lookup.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Streaming API for current status) — the Streaming API delivers event messages; it is not a way to display invoice history on a page.
Option C (custom object Invoice__c, master-detail) — stores 12 million rows in Salesforce, and master-detail would make Opportunity carry all of them.
Option D (custom object Invoice__c, lookup) — still stores the 12 million rows the question is trying to avoid.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.platform_connect_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A customer wants to maintain geographic location information including latitude and longitude in a custom object. What would a data architect recommend to satisfy this requirement?
optionA: Create formula fields with geolocation function for this requirement.
optionB: Create custom fields to maintain latitude and longitude information
optionC: Create a geolocation custom field to maintain this requirement
optionD: Recommend app exchange packages to support this requirement.
explanation:
A geolocation custom field is the recommendation. The Geolocation compound field stores latitude and longitude together and supports the DISTANCE and GEOLOCATION functions and proximity queries natively.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (formula fields with a geolocation function) — a formula cannot store user-entered coordinates.
Option B (separate custom fields for latitude and longitude) — plain number fields lose the compound behaviour and the distance functions.
Option D (AppExchange packages) — unnecessary for a built-in field type.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/compound_fields_geolocation.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custom_field_geolocate_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal containers is implementing Salesforce lead management. UC Procure lead data from multiple sources and would like to make sure lead data as company profile and location information. Which solution should a data architect recommend to make sure lead data has both profile and location information? Option
optionA: Ask sales people to search for populating company profile and location data
optionB: Run reports to identify records which does not have company profile and location data
optionC: Leverage external data providers populate company profile and location data
optionD: Export data out of Salesforce and send to another team to populate company profile and location data
explanation:
Leveraging external data providers to populate company profile and location data is the recommendation. Leads arriving from many sources will be uneven no matter how carefully the forms are built, so completeness has to come from somewhere other than the source; an external data provider appends authoritative company profile and location attributes automatically as records land, which is the only option that scales with lead volume.
This is a data-quality judgment item; Salesforce documents enrichment products rather than naming this as the answer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ask sales people to look it up) — puts a human in the path of every record.
Option B (report on records missing the data) — measures the gap accurately and closes none of it.
Option D (export to another team to populate) — a human in the path again, with a round trip added.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005132112&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers has a legacy system that captures Conferences and Venues. These Conferences can occur at any Venue. They create hundreds of thousands of Conferences per year. Historically, they have only used 20 Venues. Which two things should the data architect consider when denormalizing this data model into a single Conference object with a Venue picklist? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Limitations on master-detail relationships.
optionB: Org data storage limitations.
optionC: Bulk API limitations on picklist fields.
optionD: Standard list view in-line editing.
explanation:
Bulk API limitations on picklist fields and standard list-view inline editing are the two keyed considerations. Collapsing Venue from a related object into a picklist on Conference trades relational integrity for a value list, and the consequences are about how that value list behaves under volume: loading hundreds of thousands of Conferences a year through the Bulk API puts every Venue value through picklist handling on insert, and a picklist is inline-editable from a standard list view, so a value can be changed in bulk by anyone with edit access and no relationship to protect it.
Be aware this is a weakly constructed item. Neither keyed consideration is stated as a documented rule anywhere in Salesforce's picklist or Bulk API guidance, and the two remaining options are rejected on relevance rather than on any documented fact. The underlying design point — that twenty stable Venues are better modelled as a picklist than as a lookup that 20,000 records each point at — is sound and is documented, as concentrating that many children on one lookup target is textbook lookup skew.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (master-detail limitations) — stop applying the moment the relationship is removed.
Option B (org data storage limitations) — storage goes down, not up, when two objects become one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/managing-lookup-skew-to-avoid-record-lock-exceptions
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

corrected.note: Item defect: neither keyed consideration (Bulk API picklist limitations, list-view inline editing) corresponds to a documented Salesforce rule, and the distractors are rejected on relevance rather than fact. The key is the exam's; the item is not decidable from documentation.

question: Universal Containers (CU) is in the process of implementing an enterprise data warehouse (EDW). UC needs to extract 100 million records from Salesforce for migration to the EDW. What data extraction strategy should a data architect use for maximum performance?
optionA: Install a third-party AppExchange tool.
optionB: Call the REST API in successive queries.
optionC: Utilize PK Chunking with the Bulk API.
optionD: Use the Bulk API in parallel mode.
explanation:
PK Chunking with the Bulk API is the strategy for maximum performance. The Bulk API guide says it "splits bulk queries on large tables into chunks based on the record IDs, or primary keys, of the queried records", and recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". At 100 million records both conditions apply.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a third-party AppExchange tool) — runs on the same API and inherits the same limits.
Option B (successive REST API queries) — pages through the same full scan more slowly, one page at a time.
Option D (Bulk API in parallel mode) — parallel mode is for loads; a bulk query without chunking still issues one query across the whole table, which is what times out.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm

question: Due to security requirements, Universal Containers needs to capture specific user actions, such as login, logout, file attachment download, package install, etc. What is the recommended approach for defining a solution for this requirement?
optionA: Use a field audit trail to capture field changes.
optionB: Use a custom object and trigger to capture changes.
optionC: Use Event Monitoring to capture these changes.
optionD: Use a third-party AppExchange app to capture changes.
explanation:
Event Monitoring is the recommended approach. It exposes login, logout, download, API and package-install events through Event Log Files and real-time event objects — purpose-built for this audit requirement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Field Audit Trail) — tracks field value history, not user actions.
Option B (custom object and trigger) — triggers fire on record DML; they cannot capture login, logout or download events.
Option D (a third-party AppExchange app) — unnecessary given the native capability.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/using_resources_event_log_files.htm
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/shield/

question: Universals Containers' system administrators have been complaining that they are not able to make changes to its users' record, including moving them to new territories without getting "unable to lock row" errors. This is causing the system admins to spend hours updating user records every day. What should the data architect do to prevent the error?
optionA: Reduce number of users updated concurrently.
optionB: Enable granular locking.
optionC: Analyze Splunk query to spot offending records.
optionD: Increase CPU for the Salesforce org.
explanation:
Enabling granular locking is what prevents the error. Moving users between territories rewrites group membership, and Salesforce "locks the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates" — which is where the lock errors come from. Granular locking narrows those locks: it allows "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved", so separate role hierarchies and territory-free groups stop blocking each other.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin switches on, so on a current org the diagnosis matters more than the toggle.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (update fewer users concurrently) — trades the error for a slower process.
Option C (analyse Splunk queries) — Splunk sees logs, not the lock semantics of the group-membership tables.
Option D (more CPU for the org) — not something a customer can buy, and it would not change which tables lock.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a requirement to create an Account plan object that is related to the Account object. Each Account plan needs to have an Account object, but the accessibility requirement of the Account plan is different from the Account object. What should an Architect recommend?
optionA: Create a custom account plan object as detail with Account as mater in a master-detail relationship.
optionB: Create a custom account plan object as detail with Account as master with additional sharing rules to allow access.
optionC: Create an account plan object with a lookup relations to Account without any validation rules to enforce the Account association.
optionD: Create an account plan object with a lookup relationship to Account with validation rules to enforce the Account association.
explanation:
An Account Plan object with a lookup relationship to Account, plus validation rules to enforce the Account association, is the recommendation. A lookup lets Account Plan keep its own OWD and sharing model — the differing accessibility requirement — and a validation rule enforcing a non-null Account makes the relationship effectively required.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (master-detail with Account as master) — forces the plan to inherit the Account's sharing, violating the accessibility difference.
Option B (master-detail plus additional sharing rules) — sharing rules can only widen access on top of inherited sharing; they cannot make the detail more restrictive than its master.
Option C (lookup with no validation) — fails the "each plan must have an Account" rule.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) provides shipping services to its customers. They use Opportunities to track customer shipments. At any given time, shipping status can be one of the 10 values. UC has 200,000 Opportunity records. When creating a new field to track shipping status on opportunity, what should the architect do to improve data quality and avoid data skew?
optionA: Create a picklist field, values sorted alphabetically.
optionB: Create a Master-Detail to custom object ShippingStatus__c.
optionC: Create a Lookup to custom object ShippingStatus__c.
optionD: Create a text field and make it an external ID.
explanation:
A picklist field, with its values sorted alphabetically, is what the architect should create. A restricted picklist enforces the 10 valid values (data quality) and avoids the lookup-driven data skew that would occur if 200,000 Opportunities all pointed at one of 10 ShippingStatus__c records — about 20,000 children each.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (master-detail to ShippingStatus__c) — creates exactly that child-record concentration, and makes Opportunity a detail of a status record.
Option C (lookup to ShippingStatus__c) — the same lookup skew, with every status change re-pointing a lookup.
Option D (text field marked external ID) — provides no value control at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/managing-lookup-skew-to-avoid-record-lock-exceptions
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: UC has a roll-up summary field on Account to calculate the count of contacts associated with an account. During the account load, SF is throwing an "Unable to lock a row" error. Which solution should a data architect recommend, to resolve the error?
optionA: Leverage data loader platform API to load data.
optionB: Perform Batch job in parallel mode and reduce Batch size
optionC: Perform Batch job in serial mode and reduce batch size
optionD: Defer roll-up summary fields calculation during data migration.
explanation:
Running the batch job in serial mode with a reduced batch size is the solution. Every Contact insert has to lock its parent Account so the roll-up summary can recompute; in parallel mode, several batches can hold contacts for the same Account at once, and one of them loses the race. Serial mode processes "one batch must complete before the next batch starts", and a smaller batch holds each parent lock for less time — which is the Bulk API guide's own remedy when lock timeouts survive batch reorganisation.
The cheaper fix to reach for first, if you control the file: sort the Contacts by AccountId so all children of one Account land in the same batch, which the guide recommends before dropping to serial mode.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Data Loader via the platform API) — runs on the same APIs and changes nothing about locking.
Option B (parallel mode with smaller batches) — shrinks the window without removing the overlap between batches.
Option D (defer roll-up summary calculation) — no such control exists; deferral is for sharing calculations, not roll-ups.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: US is implementing Salesforce and will be using Salesforce to track customer complaints, provide white papers on products and provide subscription (Fee) - based support. Which license type will US users need to fulfil US's requirements?
optionA: Lightning platform starter license.
optionB: Service cloud license.
optionC: Salesforce license.
optionD: Sales cloud license
explanation:
A Service Cloud license is what the users need. The requirement that decides this is fee-based support: service contracts and entitlements are Service Cloud functionality, and the Service Cloud feature license is what turns them on for a user. Case management for the complaints and Knowledge for the white papers come with it.
Licensing is the area of Salesforce that changes most often and is packaged commercially rather than documented as a rule, so verify the current bundle against Salesforce's licence documentation before relying on this.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Lightning Platform Starter) — does not include the standard CRM service objects.
Option C (Salesforce license) — the base user licence Service Cloud sits on top of; naming it alone leaves the entitlement capability unaccounted for.
Option D (Sales Cloud license) — the wrong half of the product; no cases, entitlements or knowledge.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The architect is planning a large data migration for Universal Containers from their legacy CRM system to Salesforce. What three things should the architect consider to optimize performance of the data migration? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Review the time zones of the User loading the data.
optionB: Remove custom indexes on the data being loaded.
optionC: Determine if the legacy system is still in use.
optionD: Defer sharing calculations of the Salesforce Org.
optionE: Deactivate approval processes and workflow rules.
explanation:
Removing custom indexes on the data being loaded, deferring sharing calculations, and deactivating approval processes and workflow rules are the three keyed considerations. Two of them are documented word for word in the LDV guide's Loading Data from the API: "Use the defer sharing calculation permission to defer sharing calculations until after all data has been loaded", and "Disable Apex triggers, workflow rules, and validations during loads; investigate the use of batch Apex to process records after the load is complete". Salesforce's own Extreme Data Loading series adds that sharing rules and complex relationships should be configured after the load rather than before it.
Option B is the item's weak point: removing custom indexes before a load is not among the pre-load steps Salesforce documents. Its published lean-configuration advice covers the sharing model, sharing rules, object relationships, workflow, validation and triggers — indexes are discussed only as something to add for query speed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the loading user's time zone) — affects how date values are interpreted, not throughput.
Option C (whether the legacy system is still in use) — a cutover question, not a performance one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-2-load-into-a-lean-salesforce-configuration
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/05/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-3-suspending-events-that-fire-on-insert

corrected.note: Answer stands as keyed, but option B is unsupported: the old explanation asserted that dropping custom indexes avoids per-insert index maintenance, and that step does not appear in Salesforce's documented pre-load configuration advice.

question: Universal Containers wants to develop a dashboard in Salesforce that will allow Sales Managers to do data exploration using their mobile device (i.e., drill down into sales-related data) and have the possibility of adding ad-hoc filters while on the move. What is a recommended solution for building data exploration dashboards in Salesforce?
optionA: Create a Dashboard in an external reporting tool, export data to the tool, and add link to the dashboard in Salesforce.
optionB: Create a Dashboard in an external reporting tool, export data to the tool, and embed the dashboard in Salesforce using the Canvas toolkit.
optionC: Create a standard Salesforce Dashboard and connect it to reports with the appropriate filters.
optionD: Create a Dashboard using Analytics Cloud that will allow the user to create ad-hoc lenses and drill down.
explanation:
A dashboard built in Analytics Cloud, letting the user create ad-hoc lenses and drill down, is the recommendation. The requirement is exploration, not display: drill down, build a view on the spot, add an ad-hoc filter from a phone. CRM Analytics (Analytics Cloud) is the Salesforce product built for that interaction model, with lenses created on the fly against a dataset.
Product naming here has moved more than once — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read option D as naming the Salesforce analytics product rather than a current brand.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (external tool, link from Salesforce) — puts the data and the security model outside Salesforce and hands the user a non-native mobile experience.
Option B (external tool embedded via Canvas) — the same, with the embedding adding integration work.
Option C (standard Salesforce dashboard) — renders components from saved reports with filters an admin defined in advance; a user cannot invent a new lens from it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm

question: UC has a classic encryption for Custom fields and is leveraging weekly data reports for data backups. During the data validation of exported data UC discovered that encrypted field values are still being exported as part of data exported. What should a data architect recommend to make sure decrypted values are exported during data export?
optionA: Set a standard profile for Data Migration user, and assign view encrypted data
optionB: Create another field to copy data from encrypted field and use this field in export
optionC: Leverage Apex class to decrypt data before exporting it.
optionD: Set up a custom profile for data migration user and assign view encrypted data.
explanation:
Setting up a custom profile for the data migration user and assigning View Encrypted Data is the recommendation. Classic Encryption masks an encrypted custom field's value from anyone without the "View Encrypted Data" permission, and an export runs as the exporting user, so the export inherits that masking; granting the permission to the user that runs the weekly export is what makes the exported values readable. The reason to build a custom profile rather than reuse a standard one is that standard profiles cannot be edited — permissions on them are fixed, so there is nowhere to add it.
Worth noting: this item is about Classic Encryption, a legacy feature. Shield Platform Encryption handles the same problem through a different permission model.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a standard profile with View Encrypted Data) — standard profiles cannot be edited, so the permission cannot be added to one.
Option B (copy the value into a second, unencrypted field) — defeats the encryption entirely and doubles the exposure.
Option C (decrypt in Apex before export) — rebuilds a permission the platform already has.
References:
https://www.salesforce.com/platform/shield/
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to store product data in Salesforce, but the standard Product object does not support the more complex hierarchical structure which is currently being used in the product master system. How can UC modify the standard Product object model to support a hierarchical data structure in order to synchronize product data from the source system to Salesforce?
optionA: Create a custom lookup field on the standard Product to reference the child record in the hierarchy.
optionB: Create a custom lookup field on the standard Product to reference the parent record in the hierarchy.
optionC: Create a custom master-detail field on the standard Product to reference the child record in the hierarchy.
optionD: Create an Apex trigger to synchronize the Product Family standard picklist field on the Product object.
explanation:
A custom lookup field on the standard Product that references the parent record in the hierarchy is how UC should model it. A hierarchy is expressed by pointing each record at its parent, so a self-referential lookup on Product2 reproduces the tree from the master system, and each product's children fall out as its related list.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (lookup to the child) — can only ever record one child per product, the wrong end of a one-to-many.
Option C (master-detail to the child) — the same wrong direction, and Product2 is one of the standard objects that cannot sit on the detail side of a master-detail relationship.
Option D (trigger syncing the Product Family picklist) — Product Family is a flat category, not a hierarchy, and no trigger makes it into one.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: UC has the following system: Billing system. Customer support system. CRM system. US has been having trouble with business intelligence across the different systems. Recently US implemented a master data management (MDM) solution that will be the system of truth for the customer records. Which MDM data element is needed to allow reporting across these systems?
optionA: Global unique customer number.
optionB: Email address.
optionC: Phone number.
optionD: Full name.
explanation:
A global unique customer number is the MDM data element needed. Cross-system reporting needs a key that means the same thing in every system and never changes; the number issued by the MDM hub is the golden record's identifier, and each source system's record id maps to it, so a report can join billing, support and CRM rows for one customer. On the Salesforce side that key lives in an external ID field — indexed and upsert-able, which is what keeps the mapping usable during integration.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (email address) — an attribute a customer can change, share or duplicate; joining on it produces missed and false matches.
Option C (phone number) — the same; shared lines and reassigned numbers break the join.
Option D (full name) — the least unique of all; names collide and change.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: (Variant) Which three characteristics of a skinny table help improve report and query performance?
optionA: Skinny tables can contain frequently used fields and thereby help avoid joins.
optionB: Skinny tables can be used to create custom indexes on multi-select picklist fields.
optionC: Skinny tables provide a view across multiple objects for easy access to combined data.
optionD: Skinny tables are kept in sync with changes to data in the source tables.
optionE: Skinny tables do not include records that are available in the recycle bin.
explanation:
Containing frequently used fields to avoid joins, being kept in sync with the source tables, and omitting records in the recycle bin are the three characteristics, and all three are stated on the Skinny Tables page. Salesforce "can create skinny tables to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins" — the join avoided is between an object's base table and its custom-field table. "Skinny tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified". And they "omit soft-deleted records", so recycle-bin rows never enter a scan.
Two details worth carrying: the documented cap is 200 columns, and you cannot build one yourself — "You can't create, access, or modify skinny tables yourself"; Salesforce Customer Support enables them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (custom indexes on multi-select picklists) — invents a capability: a skinny table is a denormalised copy, not an indexing mechanism.
Option C (a view across multiple objects) — inverts the documented rule: "Skinny tables can't contain fields from other objects."
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_skinny_tables.htm

question: Get Cloudy Consulting needs to evaluate the completeness and consistency of contact information in Salesforce. Their sales reps often have incomplete information about their accounts and contacts. Additionally, they are not able to interpret the information in a consistent manner. Get Cloudy Consulting has identified certain "key" fields which are important to their sales reps. What are two actions Get Cloudy Consulting can take to review their data for completeness and consistency? (Choose two.)
optionA: Run a report which shows the last time the key fields were updated.
optionB: Run one report per key field, grouped by that field, to understand its data variability.
optionC: Run a report that shows the percentage of blanks for the important fields.
optionD: Run a process that can fill in default values for blank fields.
explanation:
Running one report per key field grouped by that field, and running a report showing the percentage of blanks for the important fields, are the two actions. The stem names two distinct qualities and each keyed option measures exactly one: completeness is the share of records where a key field is empty, which a percent-of-blanks report gives directly; consistency is whether the same real value is recorded the same way, which shows up when you group a report by a key field and see how many distinct values it has actually accumulated.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (report on when key fields were last updated) — measures staleness, a third quality nobody asked about.
Option D (fill blanks with default values) — remediation, not review: it changes the data, and makes the completeness measurement look better without any of the missing information having arrived.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question:
A custom pricing engine for a Salesforce customer has to be decided by factors with the following hierarchy:
- State in which the customer is located.
- City in which the customer is located, if available.
- Zip code in which the customer is located, if available.
Changes to this information should have minimum code changes. What should a data architect recommend to maintain this information for the custom pricing engine that is to be built in Salesforce?
optionA: Create a custom object to maintain the pricing criteria.
optionB: Assign the pricing criteria within customer pricing engine.
optionC: Maintain require pricing criteria in custom metadata types.
optionD: Configure the pricing criteria in price books.
explanation:
Maintaining the pricing criteria in custom metadata types is the recommendation. Custom Metadata Types store the State, City and Zip pricing criteria as configurable records that Apex reads at runtime, so the pricing engine adapts to new values through deployable metadata changes rather than code edits.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom object) — puts reference data in transactional storage, where it cannot be deployed with the code and needs data-load steps in every environment.
Option B (criteria inside the pricing engine) — hard-coded; every change is a code change, the opposite of the requirement.
Option D (price books) — model product pricing, not a geographic decision hierarchy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_custommetadatatypes.htm

question: Universal Containers wants to automatically archive all inactive Account data that is older than 3 years. The information does not need to remain accessible within the application. Which two methods should be recommended to meet this requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use the Force.com Workbench to export the data.
optionB: Schedule a weekly export file from the Salesforce UI.
optionC: Schedule jobs to export and delete using an ETL tool.
optionD: Schedule jobs to export and delete using the Data Loader.
explanation:
Scheduled jobs that export and delete using an ETL tool, and scheduled jobs that export and delete using the Data Loader, are the two methods. Both can run on a schedule, export the inactive Accounts off-platform and then delete them, which satisfies automatic archive-and-purge with no need for the data to remain accessible.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Workbench export) — a manual, unschedulable tool.
Option B (weekly export from the Salesforce UI) — backs up data but never deletes it, so it does not archive.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.admin_exportdata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) manages Vehicle and Service History in Salesforce. Vehicle (Vehicle__c) and Service History (Service_History__c) are both custom objects related through a lookup relationship. Every week a batch synchronization process updates the Vehicle and Service History records in Salesforce. UC has two hours of migration window every week and is facing locking issues as part of the data migration process. What should a data architect recommend to avoid locking issues without affecting performance of data migration?
optionA: Use Bulk API parallel mode for data migration
optionB: Use Bulk API serial mode for data migration
optionC: Insert the order in another custom object and use Batch Apex to move the records to Service_Order__c object.
optionD: Change the lookup configuration to "Clear the value of this field" when lookup record is deleted.
explanation:
Bulk API serial mode is the recommendation. Serial mode processes one batch at a time, preventing the parent-record lock contention that the weekly Vehicle and Service History sync hits within its short window, and it does so without changing the data model or adding a step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Bulk API parallel mode) — parallel batches touching the same Vehicle parents are what cause the locking.
Option C (insert into another object, move with batch Apex) — adds needless complexity and a second pass, and the same parent locks occur during the move.
Option D (change the lookup's delete behaviour) — addresses what happens on deletion, not load-time locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has built a custom application on Salesforce to help track shipments around the world. A majority of the shipping records are stored on premise in an external data source. UC needs shipment details to be exposed to the custom application, and the data needs to be accessible in real time. The external data source is not OData enabled, and UC does not own a middleware tool. Which Salesforce Connect procedure should a data architect use to ensure UC's requirements are met?
optionA: Write an Apex class that makes a REST callout to the external API.
optionB: Develop a process that calls an invocable web service method.
optionC: Migrate the data to Heroku and register Postgres as a data source.
optionD: Write a custom adapter with the Apex Connector Framework.
explanation:
Writing a custom adapter with the Apex Connector Framework is the Salesforce Connect procedure. The framework lets you build a custom adapter that exposes the on-premise, non-OData source as external objects in real time, without copying data or owning middleware.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Apex REST callout) — fetches data, but does not surface it as queryable external objects the custom application can bind to.
Option B (a process calling an invocable web service) — not a real-time data-virtualisation pattern; it is automation, not a data source.
Option C (migrate to Heroku, register Postgres) — copies the data, which violates the no-import, real-time goal.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_connector_start.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to capture information on how data entities are stored within the different applications and systems used within the company. For that purpose, the architecture team decided to create a data dictionary covering the main business domains within UC. Which two common techniques are used building a data dictionary to store information on how business entities are defined?
optionA: Use Salesforce Object Query Language.
optionB: Use a data definition language.
optionC: Use an entity relationship diagram.
optionD: Use the Salesforce Metadata API.
explanation:
An entity relationship diagram and the Salesforce Metadata API are the two techniques. A data dictionary needs both halves of the picture: the ERD records how the business entities relate to one another, which no schema dump gives you, and the Metadata API extracts the technical definitions — objects, fields, types, help text and the data-classification attributes on each field — so the dictionary reflects what is actually deployed.
Be aware this item is loose: option B, a data definition language, is a perfectly ordinary way to capture entity definitions in a data dictionary outside Salesforce, and the stem asks about "the different applications and systems used within the company", not about Salesforce alone. B is rejected here only because the item is scoped to Salesforce metadata in practice.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SOQL) — queries records, not schema; it cannot describe a field that holds no data yet.
Option B (a data definition language) — a legitimate technique elsewhere, and the item's weak point; not keyed because the exam scopes the dictionary to Salesforce metadata.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor B (a data definition language) is a standard data-dictionary technique for a multi-system landscape, which is what the stem describes. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

question: Universal Containers has multiple systems all containing and maintaining customer data. Although point-to-point integrations are in place, customers are complaining about consistency in the data. What solution should the data architect recommend?
optionA: Improve existing point-to-point integrations
optionB: Data cleanse each system
optionC: Perform a onetime synchronization to level set the built up inconsistencies
optionD: An MDM solution as the customer master, with centralized integrations to ensure consistency across all systems.
explanation:
An MDM solution as the customer master, with centralised integrations to ensure consistency across all systems, is the recommendation. Point-to-point integrations keep systems talking without ever deciding who is right, so every pair can drift independently; an MDM solution fixes the cause with one governed record, survivorship rules that decide which value wins, and centralised integrations so every system reads the same answer.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents governance practice rather than naming MDM as the answer here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (improve the point-to-point integrations) — makes the same architecture faster at propagating disagreement.
Option B (cleanse each system) — leaves all of them independently authoritative, which is exactly the condition producing the complaints.
Option C (a one-time synchronisation) — fixes today and nothing after it.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented Salesforce, UC is running out of storage and needs to have an archiving solution, UC would like to maintain two years of data in Salesforce and archive older data out of Salesforce. Which solution should a data architect recommend as an archiving solution?
optionA: Use a third-party backup solution to backup all data off platform.
optionB: Build a batch join move all records off platform, and delete all records from Salesforce.
optionC: Build a batch join to move two-year-old records off platform, and delete records from Salesforce.
optionD: Build a batch job to move all restore off platform, and delete old records from Salesforce.
explanation:
Build a batch job to move two-year-old records off platform and delete those records from Salesforce — that is the archiving solution. Records older than two years are moved out by the batch job and deleted from Salesforce, so two years of live data stay in the org while the storage behind everything older is reclaimed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (third-party solution copying all data off platform) — a copy frees nothing unless the records are also deleted, and it copies the two years UC wants to keep live.
Option B (batch job moving all records off platform, deleting all) — destroys the two years UC needs to keep.
Option D (batch job moving "all restore" off platform, deleting old records) — incoherent as written; a restore is not something you archive.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm

question: UC is migrating data from legacy system to SF. UC would like to preserve the following information on records being migrated: Date time stamps for created date and last modified date. Ownership of records belonging to inactive users being migrated to Salesforce. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommends to preserve the date timestamps and ownership on records? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Log a case with SF to update these fields
optionB: Enable update records with Inactive Owners Permission
optionC: Enable Set Audit fields upon Record Creation Permission
optionD: Enable modify all and view all permission.
explanation:
Enabling the Update Records with Inactive Owners permission and the Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation permission are the two solutions. Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation lets the load preserve the original CreatedDate and LastModifiedDate values, and Update Records with Inactive Owners lets records keep owners who are now inactive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (log a case with Salesforce) — unnecessary; both capabilities are self-service permissions.
Option D (Modify All and View All) — grants access to records but preserves neither audit fields nor inactive ownership.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000213290&language=en_US&type=1

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) plans to maintain contact preferences for customers and employees. NTO has implemented the following: 1. Customers are Person Accounts for their retail business. 2. Customers are represented as Contacts for their commercial business. 3. Employees are maintained as Users. 4. Prospects are maintained as Leads. NTO needs to implement a standard communication preference management model for Person Accounts, Contacts, Users, and Leads. Which option should the data architect recommend NTO to satisfy this requirement?
optionA: Create custom fields for contact preferences in Lead, Person Account, and Users objects.
optionB: Create case for contact preferences, and use this to validate the preferences for Lead, Person Accounts, and Users.
optionC: Create a custom object to maintain preferences and build relationships to Lead, Person Account, and Users.
optionD: Use Individual objects to maintain the preferences with relationships to Lead, Person Account, and Users.
explanation:
Using Individual objects to maintain the preferences, related to Lead, Person Account and User, is the recommendation. Salesforce's privacy model is built around a single standard entity rather than a preference field on each object: the Individual record is where a person's data privacy and communication preferences live, and the consent data model hangs the rest — authorization form consent, contact point consent, data use purpose — off it. Relating Leads, Person Accounts, Contacts and Users to Individual records gives one preference store that behaves the same way for every actor type.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom fields on Lead, Person Account and User) — four copies of the same preference and four places to keep them honest.
Option B (a Case per preference) — Cases are a service construct with no role in preference management.
Option C (a custom preferences object) — rebuilds Individual with none of the standard consent objects that already work with it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/data-models/guide/privacy-consent.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.individuals_store_data_privacy.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses the following Salesforce products: Sales Cloud for customer management. Marketing Cloud for marketing. Einstein Analytics for business reporting. UC occasionally gets a list of prospects from third-party source as comma-separated values (CSV) files for marketing purposes. Historically, UC would load contact Lead object in Salesforce and sync to Marketing Cloud to send marketing communications. The number of records in the Lead object has grown over time and has been consuming large amounts of storage in Sales Cloud, UC is looking for recommendations to reduce the storage and advice on how to optimize the marketing Cloud to send marketing communications. The number of records in the Lead object has grown over time and has been consuming large amounts of storage in Sales Cloud, UC is looking for recommendations to reduce the storage and advice on how to optimize the marketing process. What should a data architect recommend to UC in order to immediately avoid storage issues in the future?
optionA: Load the CSV files in Einstein Analytics and sync with Marketing Cloud prior to sending marketing communications;
