optionB: Load the CSV files in an external database and sync with Marketing Cloud prior to sending marketing communications.
optionC: Load the contacts directly to Marketing Cloud and have a reconciliation process to track prospects that are converted to customers.
optionD: Continue to use the existing process to use Lead object to sync with Marketing Cloud and delete Lead records from Sales after the sync is complete.
explanation:
Loading the contacts directly to Marketing Cloud, with a reconciliation process to track prospects that convert to customers, is the recommendation. The prospects in these CSV files are marketing audience, not sales pipeline — nobody in Sales Cloud works them until one converts — so loading them straight into Marketing Cloud puts the audience where the communications are sent from and keeps the growth out of Sales Cloud storage entirely; the reconciliation process brings across only the prospects that actually become customers.
This is a cross-cloud architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the products rather than ranking these options.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (load into Einstein Analytics and sync) — still needs a second hop into Marketing Cloud, and an analytics tool is not an audience store.
Option B (load into an external database and sync) — the same second hop, plus a system to operate.
Option D (keep loading Leads, delete after each sync) — keeps every one of the storage, automation and audit costs the stem is trying to escape, and adds a bulk delete every week.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Northern trail Outfitters (NTO) runs its entire out of an enterprise data warehouse (EDW), NTD's sales team starting to use Salesforce after a recent implementation, but currently lacks data required to advanced and opportunity to the next stage. NTO's management has research Salesforce Connect and would like to use It to virtualize and report on data from the EDW within Salesforce. NTO will be running thousands of reports per day across 10 to 15 external objects. What should a data architect consider before implementing Salesforce Connect for reporting?
optionA: Maximum number for records returned
optionB: OData callout limits per day
optionC: Maximum page size for server-driven paging
optionD: Maximum external objects per org
explanation:
OData callout limits per day are what to consider first. External objects hold no data — every report row is fetched live by a web-service callout to the EDW at the moment the report runs. Thousands of reports a day across 10 to 15 external objects therefore turns directly into callout volume, and Salesforce meters it: "Depending on your qualified Salesforce organization edition, specific governor limits are in place for number of allowed callouts per hour and per day." Exceed them and the org becomes "temporarily unable to access external data sources through Salesforce Connect" — reporting stops org-wide, not just for the offending report.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (maximum records returned) — a real limit, but per query; it does not scale with how many times a day the reports run.
Option C (maximum page size for server-driven paging) — a per-request detail, not a daily budget.
Option D (maximum external objects per org) — 10 to 15 objects is nowhere near the ceiling, and the ceiling does not move with report volume.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000382494&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.odata_general_limits.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a very large and complex Salesforce org with hundreds of validation rules and triggers. The triggers are responsible for system updates and data manipulation as records are created or updates by users. A majority of the automation tool within UC'' org were not designed to run during a data load. UC is importing 100,000 records into Salesforce across several objects over the weekend. What should a data architect do to mitigate any unwanted results during the import?
optionA: Ensure validation rules, triggers and other automation tools are disabled.
optionB: Ensure duplication and matching rules and defined.
optionC: Import the data in smaller batches over a 24-hour period.
optionD: Bulkify the trigger to handle import leads.
explanation:
Ensuring validation rules, triggers and other automation tools are disabled is what mitigates unwanted results. Because the org's automation was not designed to run during a load, disabling it before importing 100,000 records prevents unintended updates, errors and side effects — the LDV guide's own advice for loads.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (define duplicate and matching rules) — does not address the automation risk; it adds another rule that fires during the load.
Option C (smaller batches over 24 hours) — the automation still fires on every record, just more slowly.
Option D (bulkify the trigger for import leads) — covers one trigger, not the hundreds of validation rules and triggers the stem describes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/05/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-3-suspending-events-that-fire-on-insert

question: Universal Containers is creating a new B2C service offering for consumers to ship goods across continents. This is in addition to their well-established B2B offering. Their current Salesforce org uses the standard Account object to track B2B customers. They are expecting to have over 50,000,000 consumers over the next five years across their 50 business regions. B2C customers will be individuals. Household data is not required to be stored. What is the recommended data model for consumer account data to be stored in Salesforce?
optionA: Use the Account object with Person Accounts and a new B2C page layout.
optionB: Use the Account object with a newly created Record Type for B2C customers.
optionC: Create a new picklist value for B2C customers on the Account Type field.
optionD: Use 50 umbrella Accounts for each region, with customers as associated Contacts.
explanation:
The Account object with Person Accounts and a new B2C page layout is the recommended model. Person Accounts model 50 million individual consumers natively while letting B2B business Accounts coexist, and a B2C page layout tailors the UI; Person Accounts scale to tens of millions of records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a B2C Record Type on Account) — a record type does not give a person-centric model; the consumer still has no Contact-level identity.
Option C (a B2C value on the Account Type picklist) — the same, with even less structure.
Option D (50 umbrella Accounts with consumers as Contacts) — a million Contacts per region under one parent is massive account data skew.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has a variety of customers that include householder, businesses, and individuals. The following conditions exist within its system: NTO has a total of five million customers. Duplicate records exist, which is replicated across many systems, including Salesforce. Given these conditions, there is a lack of consistent presentation and clear identification of a customer record. Which three option should a data architect perform to resolve the issues with the customer data?
optionA: Create a unique global customer ID for each customer and store that in all system for referential identity.
optionB: Use Salesforce CDC to sync customer data cross all systems to keep customer record in sync.
optionC: Invest in data duplicate tool to de-dupe and merge duplicate records across all systems.
optionD: Duplicate customer records across the system and provide a two-way sync of data between the systems.
optionE: Create a customer master database external to Salesforce as a system of truth and sync the customer data with all systems.
explanation:
Creating a unique global customer ID stored in every system, investing in a de-duplication tool to merge duplicates across all systems, and creating an external customer master as the system of truth are the three actions. The global ID gives referential identity across systems, the de-dupe and merge tool resolves the existing duplicates, and the external customer master synced to all systems sustains a single consistent record going forward.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Salesforce CDC to sync across systems) — Change Data Capture publishes Salesforce changes; it does not de-duplicate, and it makes Salesforce the hub when the stem needs a neutral master.
Option D (duplicate records across systems with two-way sync) — worsens the problem: more copies, and conflicts propagated in both directions.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: NTO need to extract 50 million records from a custom object everyday from its Salesforce org. NTO is facing query timeout issues while extracting these records. What should a data architect recommend in order to get around the time out issue?
optionA: Use a custom auto number and formula field and use that to chunk records while extracting data.
optionB: The REST API to extract data as it automatically chunks records by 200.
optionC: Use ETL tool for extraction of records.
optionD: Ask SF support to increase the query timeout value.
explanation:
Using a custom auto-number and formula field to chunk records while extracting is the recommendation. A query timeout on a 50-million-row extract is a selectivity problem, and Salesforce publishes the technique that fixes it. Its LDV extraction guidance has you create an auto-number field with "Generate Auto Number for existing records" enabled, add a numeric formula field over it — because "you cannot use an index with comparison operators such as '<=' or '>' for the text-based auto-number field" — have Support index that formula field, then extract in ranges: WHERE ExportID__c > 1000000 AND ExportID__c <= 1200000. Each query stays under the index selectivity threshold, so none of them times out.
On a current org, PK Chunking with the Bulk API does the same job with no custom fields, and Salesforce recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". It is not among the options here, but it is what you would reach for first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (REST API chunking by 200) — the REST API does not chunk queries; that number is a query-locator page size and has nothing to do with query execution time.
Option C (an ETL tool) — how you would orchestrate and schedule the extract, but on its own it issues the same unselective SOQL against the same 50 million rows and hits the same timeout; the chunking is the fix, not the tool.
Option D (ask Support to raise the timeout) — the SOQL query timeout is not a value Salesforce Support raises on request.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/06/extracting-large-data-volume-ldv-in-force-com
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

corrected.note: Key moved C to A. Salesforce's own large-data-volume extraction guidance documents the auto-number plus indexed formula field as the chunking technique for exactly this failure, while an ETL tool by itself issues the same unselective query and hits the same timeout. The old explanation dismissed the documented technique as "fragile to build".

question: What 2 data management policies does the data classification feature allow customers to classify in Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Reference data policy.
optionB: Data governance policy.
optionC: Data sensitivity level
optionD: Compliance categorization policy.
explanation:
Data sensitivity level and compliance categorization are the two policies. Salesforce Data Classification lets customers classify fields by Data Sensitivity Level and by Compliance Categorization (alongside Data Owner and Field Usage).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (reference data policy) — not a classification dimension the feature exposes.
Option B (data governance policy) — the programme that uses the classifications, not a field attribute.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Container has a Sales Cloud implementation for a sales team and an enterprise resource planning (ERP) as a customer master. Sales team are complaining about duplicate account and data quality issues with account data. Which two solutions should a data architect recommend to resolve the complaints?
optionA: Build a nightly batch job to de-dupe data, and merge account records.
optionB: Integrate Salesforce with ERP, and make ERP as system of truth.
optionC: Build a nightly sync job from ERP to Salesforce.
optionD: Implement a de-dupe solution and establish account ownership in Salesforce
explanation:
Integrating Salesforce with the ERP and making the ERP the system of truth, and implementing a de-dupe solution with account ownership established in Salesforce, are the two solutions. Two different causes need two different fixes: the disagreement about which Account is right comes from having no authority, which naming the ERP the system of truth settles; the duplicates already in Salesforce, and the ones reps will create tomorrow, need a de-duplication solution plus clear account ownership so somebody is accountable for each record.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents duplicate management and integration mechanisms rather than ranking these pairings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (nightly batch de-dupe and merge) — cleans up after a cause nobody addressed, every night, forever.
Option C (nightly one-way sync from ERP) — half of B: it moves data without establishing that the ERP's version wins, so conflicts persist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: During the implementation of Salesforce, a customer has the following requirements for Sales Orders: 1. Sales Order information needs to be shown to users in Salesforce. 2. Sales Orders are maintained in the on-premises enterprise resource planning (ERP). 3. Sales Order information has more than 150 million records. 4. Sales Orders will not be updated in Salesforce. What should a data architect recommend for maintaining Sales Orders in Salesforce?
optionA: Use custom objects to maintain Sales Orders in Salesforce.
optionB: Use custom big objects to maintain Sales Orders in Salesforce.
optionC: Use external objects to maintain Sales Order in Salesforce.
optionD: Use Standard order object to maintain Sale Orders in Salesforce
explanation:
External objects are the recommendation for maintaining Sales Orders in Salesforce. With more than 150 million read-only Sales Orders that live in the on-premise ERP and are never updated in Salesforce, external objects virtualise them via OData with no storage cost and always-current data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom objects) — stores 150 million rows on-platform, for data that is owned and maintained elsewhere.
Option B (custom big objects) — still on-platform storage and a copy to keep in sync; big objects are for data Salesforce holds, not data the ERP owns.
Option D (the standard Order object) — on-platform storage again, and its automation and sharing are wasted on records nobody edits.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm

question: Get Cloudy Consulting monitors 15,000 servers, and these servers automatically record their status every 10 minutes. Because of company policy, these status reports must be maintained for 5 years. Managers at Get Cloudy Consulting need access to up to one week's worth of these status reports with all of their details. An Architect is recommending what data should be integrated into Salesforce and for how long it should be stored in Salesforce. Which two limits should the Architect be aware of? (Choose two.)
optionA: Data storage limits
optionB: Workflow rule limits
optionC: API Request limits
optionD: Webservice callout limits
explanation:
Data storage limits and API request limits are the two limits to be aware of. Storing five years of status reports from 15,000 servers reporting every 10 minutes is bounded by data storage, and continuously ingesting that volume through an integration is bounded by the daily API request allocation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (workflow rule limits) — no workflow is described; the rules cap does not govern storage or ingestion.
Option D (web-service callout limits) — callouts are outbound from Salesforce; the status reports are being pushed in.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet.meta/salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet/salesforce_app_limits_platform_api.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has implemented Salesforce for its sales users. The opportunity management in Salesforce Is implemented as follows: 1. Sales users enter their opportunities in Salesforce for forecasting and reporting purposes. 2. NTO has a product pricing system (PPS) that is used to update the Opportunity Amount field on opportunities on a daily basis. 3. PPS is the trusted source within NTO for Opportunity Amount. 4. NTO uses Opportunity Forecast for its sales planning and management. Sales users have noticed that their updates to the Opportunity Amount field are overwritten when PPS updates their opportunities. How should a data architect address this overwriting issue?
optionA: Create a custom field for Opportunity amount that PSS updates separating the field sales user updates.
optionB: Change PSS integration to update only Opportunity Amount field when the value is null.
optionC: Change Opportunity Amount field access to Read Only for sales users field-level security.
optionD: Create a custom field for Opportunity amount that sales users update separating the field that PPS updates.
explanation:
Changing the Opportunity Amount field to Read Only for sales users through field-level security is how to address the overwriting. The stem already names PPS as the trusted source for Opportunity Amount, so the design question is not who wins but how to stop the argument; removing edit access at the platform level does that, and Forecasts keep reading the same standard Amount field they always did.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom field for PPS to update) — leaves the standard Amount, the field Opportunity Forecasting actually uses, populated by the sales users rather than the trusted source.
Option B (PPS writes only when Amount is null) — hands authority to whoever types first, the opposite of what the stem says PPS is for.
Option D (a custom field for sales users to update) — keeps the trusted number in Amount, but the sales users' input then goes nowhere the forecast can see, and the stem never asks for it to be kept.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: UC needs to load a large volume of leads into Salesforce on a weekly basis. During this process the validation rules are disabled. What should a data architect recommend to ensure data quality is maintained in Salesforce.
optionA: Activate validation rules once the leads are loaded into Salesforce to maintain quality.
optionB: Allow validation rules to be activated during the load of leads into Salesforce.
optionC: Develop custom APEX batch process to improve quality once the load is completed.
optionD: Ensure the lead data is preprocessed for quality before loading into Salesforce.
explanation:
Ensuring the lead data is preprocessed for quality before loading into Salesforce is the recommendation. Because validation rules are disabled during the weekly load, the only reliable way to maintain quality is to validate the data before it enters the org.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (activate validation rules after the load) — the bad data is already saved; rules only evaluate future edits.
Option B (leave validation rules active during the load) — rows fail mid-load and the load itself is what the rules were disabled to protect.
Option C (custom batch Apex clean-up afterwards) — reactive and incomplete, and it re-implements the rules that already exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/05/extreme-force-com-data-loading-part-3-suspending-events-that-fire-on-insert

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Salesforce Sales & Service Cloud for B2C sales and customer service but they are experiencing a lot of duplicate customers in the system. Which are two recommended approaches for UC to avoid duplicate data and increase the level of data quality?
optionA: Use Duplicate Management.
optionB: Use an Enterprise Service Bus.
optionC: Use Data.com Clean
optionD: Use a data warehouse.
explanation:
Duplicate Management and Data.com Clean are the two keyed approaches. Native Duplicate Management is the platform answer: matching rules decide what counts as the same customer and duplicate rules alert or block at the moment of entry, in the UI and through the API, without code.
Option C names Data.com Clean, which Salesforce has retired — it appears in the Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and its setup article no longer exists. Keep C as the keyed answer because that is what the item tests, but the current equivalent is a third-party enrichment and cleansing service or Data Cloud, and the point that survives is the design one: preventing duplicates at entry and standardising incoming values are two different jobs, and a duplicate rule only does the first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an Enterprise Service Bus) — moves messages between systems; it neither compares two customer records nor prevents a third.
Option D (a data warehouse) — stores copies for analysis; it does nothing about duplicates at the point of entry.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005132112&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Answer stands as the exam keys it, but the item is stale: keyed option C names Data.com Clean, a product Salesforce has retired.

question: Universal Containers uses Apex jobs to create leads in Salesforce. The business team has requested that lead creation failures should be reported to them. Which option does Apex provide to report errors from this Apex job?
optionA: Use Custom Object to store leads, and allow unprocessed leads to be reported.
optionB: Save Apex errors in a custom object, and allow access to this object for reporting.
optionC: Use Apex services to email failures to business when error occurs.
optionD: Use AppExchange package to clean lead information before Apex job processes them.
explanation:
Using Apex services to email failures to the business when an error occurs is the keyed option. Apex can report its own failures by email — a batch job marked Database.Stateful can accumulate failed rows across execute() calls and send them from finish() with Messaging.SingleEmailMessage, which puts the errors in front of the business team without anyone logging into Salesforce.
Be aware this item is weakly constructed. Option B — writing Apex errors to a custom object and reporting on it — is the pattern most production orgs actually use, because it survives inbox rules and supports trend reporting, and it is a direct answer to "errors should be reported to them". Nothing in the stem chooses between push and pull, so both B and C are defensible.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (store leads in a custom object, report the unprocessed ones) — records what did not get processed but reports no reason.
Option B (save Apex errors to a custom object for reporting) — a sound pattern and the item's weak point; not keyed because the exam wants the push mechanism.
Option D (AppExchange package to clean lead data first) — reduces failures rather than reporting them.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor B (log Apex errors to a custom object and report on it) answers the stem as well as the keyed option C does, and nothing in the question distinguishes a pushed notification from a queryable error log.

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to ensure their data on 100,000 Accounts pertaining mostly to US-based companies is enriched and cleansed on an ongoing basis. UC is looking for a solution that allows easy monitoring of key data quality metrics. What should be the recommended solution to meet this requirement?
optionA: Use a declarative approach by installing and configuring Data.com Clean to monitor Account data quality.
optionB: Implement Batch Apex that calls out a third-party data quality API in order to monitor Account data quality.
optionC: Use declarative approach by installing and configuring Data.com Prospector to monitor Account data quality.
optionD: Implement an Apex Trigger on Account that queries a third-party data quality API to monitor Account data quality.
explanation:
Installing and configuring Data.com Clean to monitor Account data quality is the keyed answer, and the product no longer exists. The requirement has two halves — ongoing enrichment and cleansing of 100,000 Accounts, and easy monitoring of data quality metrics — and the item wants the declarative option that covers both rather than code that covers one. But Data.com appears in Salesforce's Past Product & Feature Retirements list and its setup article is gone, so as printed this question has no correct answer on a current org. The durable point is the shape of the right solution: a configured, scheduled enrichment service that writes back match and fill status you can report on, which today means a third-party data quality service or Data Cloud rather than anything native.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Batch Apex calling a third-party API) — means building and maintaining an integration, plus whatever reporting you write on top of it.
Option C (Data.com Prospector) — the wrong half of the old product pair: it adds new records rather than cleaning existing ones.
Option D (an Account trigger calling a third-party API) — code again, and a synchronous callout on every save is the wrong shape for ongoing enrichment.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005132112&language=en_US&type=1
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item is stale beyond repair: the keyed answer A is Data.com Clean, a retired product, and no remaining option is correct on a current org. Kept as keyed because that is what the exam tests.

question: Universal Containers is setting up an external Business Intelligence (BI) system and wants to extract 1,000,000 Contact records. What should be recommended to avoid timeouts during the export process?
optionA: Use the SOAP API to export data.
optionB: Utilize the Bulk API to export the data.
optionC: Use GZIP compression to export the data.
optionD: Schedule a Batch Apex job to export the data.
explanation:
Utilising the Bulk API to export the data is the recommendation. The LDV guide's extraction advice points straight at it: when a query could return over a million records, evaluate Bulk API 2.0's query capability. It runs asynchronously and returns results in batches, so the extract never sits inside a synchronous request waiting to time out.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SOAP API) — holds a synchronous connection open for a query it was never sized for.
Option C (GZIP compression) — makes the response smaller on the wire and changes nothing about how long the query takes to run server-side.
Option D (Batch Apex) — processes records inside Salesforce; it is not an export path to an external BI system.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_extracting_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm

question: For a production cutover, a large number of Account records will be loaded into Salesforce from a legacy system. The legacy system does not have enough information to determine the Ownership for these Accounts upon initial load. Which two recommended options assign Account ownership to mitigate potential performance problems?
optionA: Let a "system user" own all the Account records without assigning any role to this user in Role Hierarchy.
optionB: Let a "system user" own the Account records and assign this user to the lowest-level role in the Role Hierarchy.
optionC: Let the VP of the Sales department, who will report directly to the senior VP, own all the Account records.
optionD: Let a "system user" own all the Account records and make this user part of the highest-level role in the Role Hierarchy.
explanation:
A system user owning all the Accounts with no role in the hierarchy, or a system user in the highest-level role, are the two recommended options. One user owning every loaded Account is ownership data skew — Salesforce defines it as "a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object" — and the cost lands on sharing recalculation. The documented mitigation is exact. First choice: "If you do have a compelling reason for assigning ownership to a small number of users, you can minimize possible performance impacts by not assigning the users to a role". If the user must have a role, "Place them in a separate role at the top of the hierarchy", then "Don't move them out of that top-level role to avoid triggering sharing recalculations". The same page adds a third rule worth remembering: "Keep them out of public groups that can be used as the source for sharing rules."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (system user in the lowest-level role) — the opposite of what is documented: every role above it inherits access to all of those records, so the sharing tables carry an entry for each ancestor and every recalculation walks the whole hierarchy.
Option C (the VP of Sales owns them) — worse still: a real VP reporting to a senior VP sits mid-hierarchy and is a person whose role will actually change.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

corrected.note: Key moved A,B to A,D. Salesforce's Ownership Data Skew page says to place a heavy-owning user in "a separate role at the top of the hierarchy" when a role is unavoidable. The deck keyed the lowest-level role, which is the placement that maximises sharing-table entries because every role above inherits access to all the records.

question: Universal Containers keeps its Account data in Salesforce and its Invoice data in a third-party ERP system. They have connected the Invoice data through a Salesforce external object. They want data from both Accounts and Invoices visible in one report in one place. What two approaches should an architect suggest for achieving this solution? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create a report in an external system combining Salesforce Account data and Invoice data from the ERP.
optionB: Create a report combining data from the Account standard object and the Invoices external object.
optionC: Create a Visualforce page combining Salesforce Account data and Invoice external object data.
optionD: Create a separate Salesforce report for Accounts and Invoices and combine them in a dashboard.
explanation:
A report in an external system combining Salesforce Account data with Invoice data from the ERP, and a Visualforce page combining Account data with the Invoice external object, are the two keyed approaches. The external BI report reads Account data from Salesforce and Invoice data from the ERP directly, with no dependency on the external-object layer at all. The Visualforce page queries the Account and the Invoice external object together and renders them as one view inside Salesforce.
Option B is the interesting one. Salesforce does support reporting on external objects — it publishes an article titled "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports" — so a custom report type spanning Account and an Invoices external object is possible in principle. It needs an external lookup or indirect lookup relationship between them, which this stem never says exists, and reports that touch an external object are bounded in how many rows they fetch and depend on the ERP responding while the report runs. That is why A and C are the safer recommendations here, not because native reporting on external objects is impossible.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a report combining Account and the Invoices external object) — possible only with an external or indirect lookup the stem never establishes, and bounded by callout limits and the ERP's availability.
Option D (separate reports combined on a dashboard) — two reports side by side is explicitly not the single combined report the stem asks for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.platform_connect_considerations_reports.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands, but the old explanation asserted that "Salesforce cannot natively report across a standard object and an external object together" — an invented absence. Salesforce publishes "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports"; option B is possible given a lookup relationship, so this item has three defensible options rather than two.

question: As part of a phased Salesforce rollout, there will be 3 deployments spread out over the year. The requirements have been carefully documented. Which two methods should an architect use to trace back configuration changes to the detailed requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Review the setup audit trail for configuration changes.
optionB: Put the business purpose in the Description of each field.
optionC: Maintain a data dictionary with the justification for each field.
optionD: Use the Force.com IDE to save the metadata files in source control.
explanation:
Putting the business purpose in each field's Description, and saving the metadata files in source control with the Force.com IDE, are the two keyed methods. Traceability needs the reason to travel with the thing that changed: a field's Description holds its business purpose on the metadata itself, so it survives every deployment and is visible to whoever finds the field later; metadata files in source control record exactly what changed in each of the three releases, and the commit history carries the why alongside it.
Be aware this item is loose: option C, a data dictionary holding the justification for each field, is a direct answer to "trace back configuration changes to the detailed requirements" and is a technique Salesforce's own governance guidance recommends. Nothing in the stem separates it from B, so three of the four options are defensible.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the setup audit trail) — a genuine record of what changed and when, but it captures no link to a requirement: it says a field was created and by whom, never which requirement asked for it.
Option C (a data dictionary with each field's justification) — a sound technique and the item's weak point; not keyed only because the exam pairs Description with source control.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor C (maintain a data dictionary with the justification for each field) answers the stem as directly as keyed option B, and Salesforce's governance guidance recommends exactly that. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

question: Universal Containers is establishing a call center that will use Salesforce. UC receives 10 million calls and creates 100 million cases every month. Cases are linked to a custom call object using lookup relationship. UC would like to run reports and dashboard to better understand different case types being created on calls to better serve customers. What solution should a data architect recommend to meet the business requirement?
optionA: Archive records to a data warehouse and run analytics on the data warehouse.
optionB: Leverage big objects to archive records and Einstein Analytics to run reports.
optionC: Leverage custom objects to store aggregate data and run analytics.
optionD: Leverage out-of-the-box reports and dashboard on case and interactive voice response (IVR) custom object.
explanation:
Leveraging big objects to archive the records and Einstein Analytics to run reports is the recommendation. One hundred million cases a month is far outside what the transactional store is designed to report on, and big objects are the platform's answer to that shape — "consistent performance, whether you have 1 million records, 100 million, or even 1 billion", with "Historical archive" and "360° view of the customer" as their named use cases. Archive the case volume there and run the analysis on the analytics platform.
One implementation detail: Salesforce does not have you report directly off a big object. View Big Object Data in Reports and Dashboards has you extract a representative subset — with Bulk API or batch Apex — into a custom object or dataset, and analyse that.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (archive to a data warehouse and analyse there) — works, but takes the data off-platform, which the stem does not ask for.
Option C (custom objects holding aggregate data) — means building and maintaining the aggregation yourself, and loses the detail behind it.
Option D (out-of-the-box reports on Case and the IVR object) — the thing that has already stopped working at this volume.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object_query_and_report.htm

question: (Variant) Universal Containers is experiencing frequent and persistent group membership locking issues that severely restricts its ability to manage manual and a automated updates at the same time. What should a data architect do in order to restore the issue?
optionA: Enable granular locking
optionB: Enable parallel sharing rule calculation.
optionC: Enable defer sharing calculation
optionD: Enable implicit sharing
explanation:
Enabling granular locking is what resolves persistent group-membership locking. Those lock errors come from the sharing system locking "the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates". Granular locking narrows the locks so "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved" — which is exactly what lets a manual update and an automated one run at the same time.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin turns on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (parallel sharing rule calculation) — speeds recalculation of sharing rules, a different operation from group membership maintenance.
Option C (defer sharing calculation) — a planned bulk-window tool: suspend recalculation, do the work, resume. It does not make two concurrent membership updates compatible.
Option D (implicit sharing) — how Salesforce grants parent access from child records; no bearing on locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: NTO has decided to franchise its brand. Upon implementation, 1000 franchisees will be able to access NTO's product information and track large customer sales and opportunities through a portal. The Franchisees will also be able to run monthly and quarterly sales reports and projections as well as view the reports in dashboards. Which licenses does NTO need to provide these features to the Franchisees?
optionA: Salesforce Sales Cloud license
optionB: Lightning Platform license
optionC: Customer Community license
optionD: Partner Community license
explanation:
Partner Community licenses are what NTO needs for the franchisees. Franchisees tracking customer sales and opportunities are partners, not customers, and that distinction is what the licence split is built on: the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries leads, opportunities, campaigns and quotes, along with reports and dashboards in the site.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales Cloud license) — an internal-employee licence; not something to buy a thousand times over for external franchisees.
Option B (Lightning Platform license) — custom apps without the standard CRM sales objects the franchisees need.
Option C (Customer Community license) — built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and does not extend to leads and opportunities.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has deployed Salesforce to manage Marketing, Sales, and Support efforts in a multi-system ERP environment. After reaching the limits of native reports & dashboards, UC leadership is looking to understand what options can be used to provide more analytical insights. What two approaches should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: AppExchange Apps
optionB: Wave Analytics
optionC: Weekly Snapshots
optionD: Setup Audit Trails
explanation:
AppExchange apps and Wave Analytics are the two approaches. Once native reports and dashboards have hit their ceiling, the two directions that add real analytical capability are the Salesforce analytics platform — CRM Analytics, named here by its older brand — which brings datasets, lenses and exploration beyond what a report can express, and purpose-built analytics apps from AppExchange that package models and dashboards for a domain.
The product in option B has been renamed several times — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read it as naming the Salesforce analytics platform rather than a current brand.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (weekly snapshots) — a way to accumulate history for trending; useful, but they add data, not analytical capability.
Option D (Setup Audit Trail) — records configuration changes; nothing to do with business insight.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm

question: North Trail Outfitters (NTD) is in the process of evaluating big objects to store large amounts of asset data from an external system. NTO will need to report on this asset data weekly. Which two native tools should a data architect recommend to achieve this reporting requirement?
optionA: Standard reports and dashboards
optionB: Async SOQL with a custom object
optionC: Standard SOQL queries
optionD: Einstein Analytics
explanation:
Async SOQL with a custom object, and Einstein Analytics, are the two keyed native tools. Big objects sit outside the standard reporting path; Salesforce's own guidance is that at this scale "it's not practical to build reports or dashboards directly from that data" — you extract a representative subset into a custom object and report on that, or feed the analytics platform and analyse it there.
Read option B for the pattern, not the tool it names. Async SOQL was retired in Summer '23: Salesforce's retirement notice states "You must use the Bulk API or batch Apex to query or report on custom Big Objects after your org gets upgraded to the Summer '23 release." The aggregate-into-a-custom-object approach is still right; the mechanism is now Bulk API or batch Apex.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (standard reports and dashboards) — cannot be pointed at a big object.
Option C (standard SOQL queries) — synchronous SOQL on a big object is confined to its index fields with equality and range filters only, a lookup mechanism rather than a reporting one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000394892&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object_query_and_report.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/big_object_querying.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands as keyed, but keyed option B names Async SOQL, which Salesforce retired in Summer '23 and replaced with Bulk API or batch Apex for querying and reporting on big objects.

question: Universal Containers is looking to use Salesforce to manage their sales organization. They will be migrating legacy account data from two aging systems into Salesforce. Which two design considerations should an architect take to minimize data duplication? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use a workflow to check and prevent duplicates.
optionB: Clean data before importing to Salesforce.
optionC: Use Salesforce matching and duplicate rules.
optionD: Import the data concurrently.
explanation:
Cleaning the data before importing, and using Salesforce matching and duplicate rules, are the two design considerations. Cleansing and de-duplicating in the source or staging step before load removes duplicates and bad data up front, and native matching and duplicate rules catch cross-system collisions at insert time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a workflow to check and prevent duplicates) — workflow cannot compare a record against existing ones, block a save, or merge.
Option D (import the data concurrently) — increases, rather than reduces, the chance of creating duplicates, since neither load can see what the other is inserting.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Two million Opportunities need to be loaded in different batches into Salesforce using the Bulk API in parallel mode. What should an Architect consider when loading the Opportunity records?
optionA: Use the Name field values to sort batches.
optionB: Order batches by Auto-number field.
optionC: Create indexes on Opportunity object text fields.
optionD: Group batches by the AccountId field.
explanation:
Grouping batches by the AccountId field is the consideration. Grouping Opportunity records so all children of the same Account fall in one batch prevents two parallel batches from locking the same parent Account, which is the lock contention parallel mode otherwise produces — and it is the Bulk API guide's own advice before dropping to serial mode.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sort batches by Name) — scatters children of the same parent across batches.
Option B (order batches by an auto-number) — the same; the auto-number has no relation to the parent.
Option C (indexes on Opportunity text fields) — indexes speed reads and do nothing for write-time locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing its new Internet of Things technology, which consists of smart containers that provide information on container temperature and humidity, updated every 10 minutes back to UC. There are roughly 10,000 containers equipped with this technology with the number expected to increase to 50,000 across the next five years. It is essential that Salesforce user have access to current and historical temperature and humidity data for each container. What is the recommended solution?
optionA: Create new custom fields for temperature and humidity in the existing Container custom object, as well as an external ID field that is unique for each container. These custom fields are updated when a new measure is received.
optionB: Create a new Container Reading custom object, which is created when a new measure is received for a specific container. The Container Reading custom object has a master-detail relationship to the container object.
optionC: Create a new Lightning Component that displays last humidity and temperature data for a specific container and can also display historical trends obtaining relevant data from UC's existing data warehouse.
optionD: Create a new Container Reading custom object with a master-detail relationship to Container which is created when a new measure is received for a specific container. Implement an archiving process that runs every hour.
explanation:
A Container Reading custom object in a master-detail relationship to Container, created for each measure received, with an archiving process that runs every hour, is the recommended solution. The stem requires historical readings as well as current ones, so the readings have to be their own records; the archiving process is what keeps that viable. Fifty thousand containers reporting every ten minutes is 144 readings per container per day, so each Container passes 10,000 children in under three months, and Salesforce's own guidance is to "Distribute child records so that no parent has more than 10,000 child records" — which makes archiving part of the design rather than an optimisation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (temperature and humidity fields on Container, overwritten each reading) — keeps only the latest value; the history the stem requires is lost on every update.
Option B (Container Reading child object with no archiving) — the same model without the archiving, so it walks into parent-child data skew on every container within months.
Option C (a Lightning component reading from the warehouse) — solves the display problem and never stores the current reading in Salesforce at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_general.htm

question: To avoid creating duplicate Contacts, a customer frequently uses Data Loader to upsert Contact records into Salesforce. What common error should the data architect be aware of when using upsert?
optionA: Errors with duplicate external Id values within the same CSV file.
optionB: Errors with records being updated and inserted in the same CSV file.
optionC: Errors when a duplicate Contact name is found cause upsert to fail.
optionD: Errors with using the wrong external Id will cause the load to fail.
explanation:
Errors from duplicate external ID values within the same CSV file are the common upsert error. Upsert matches on the External ID; if the same file contains two rows with the same External ID value, Data Loader cannot decide which record to map to and throws a "Duplicate value found" / "Duplicate Id Specified" error for those rows.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (updates and inserts in the same file) — exactly what upsert is designed to handle; not an error.
Option C (a duplicate Contact name fails the upsert) — upsert matches on the external ID, not on name; a name collision does nothing by itself.
Option D (the wrong external ID fails the whole load) — a wrong or unmatched external ID value simply inserts a new record, and Data Loader reports per row rather than failing the load.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Which two aspects of data does an Enterprise data governance program aim to improve?
optionA: Data integrity
optionB: Data distribution
optionC: Data usability
optionD: Data modeling
explanation:
Data integrity and data usability are the two aspects a governance programme aims to improve. A governance programme exists to make data trustworthy and useful: integrity is the trustworthy half — accuracy, consistency and validity of the values themselves — and usability is the other half — data that people can find, interpret the same way and reuse, which is why governance produces things like a data dictionary and field-level classification rather than only validation rules.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (data distribution) — how data gets moved between systems; shaped by governance decisions, not an outcome the programme is measured on.
Option D (data modeling) — how data gets built; the same.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: DreamHouse Realty has a Salesforce org that is used to manage Contacts. What are two things an Architect should consider using to maintain data quality in this situation? (Choose two.)
optionA: Use the private sharing model.
optionB: Use Salesforce duplicate management.
optionC: Use validation rules on new record create and edit.
optionD: Use workflow to delete duplicate records.
explanation:
Salesforce duplicate management, and validation rules on record create and edit, are the two things to consider. Duplicate Management prevents or flags duplicate Contacts through matching and duplicate rules, and validation rules enforce data-entry standards on create and edit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a private sharing model) — controls visibility, not quality.
Option D (workflow to delete duplicates) — workflow rules cannot delete records, and they cannot detect duplicates either.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing a new customer categorization process where customers should be assigned to a Gold, Silver, or Bronze category if they've purchased UC's new support service. Customers are expected to be evenly distributed across all three categories. Currently, UC has around 500,000 customers, and is expecting 1% of existing non-categorized customers to purchase UC's new support service every month over the next five years. What is the recommended solution to ensure long-term performance, bearing in mind the above requirements?
optionA: Implement a new global picklist custom field with Gold, Silver, and Bronze values and enable it in Account.
optionB: Implement a new picklist custom field in the Account object with Gold, Silver, and Bronze values.
optionC: Implement a new Categories custom object and a master-detail relationship from Account to Category.
optionD: Implement a new Categories custom object and create a lookup field from Account to Category.
explanation:
A picklist custom field on the Account object with Gold, Silver and Bronze values is the recommended solution. A picklist with three values stores the category directly on the Account, filters and groups easily, and avoids the lookup skew a Category object would create — roughly 167,000 accounts pointing at each of three Category records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a global picklist enabled on Account) — works, but a global value set is for values shared across several objects; for three values on one object it adds indirection without benefit, which is why the exam keys the local picklist.
Option C (Categories object, master-detail from Account) — concentrates hundreds of thousands of children under each of three parents, and Account cannot be the detail of a custom object anyway.
Option D (Categories object, lookup from Account) — the same lookup skew, with the record-locking problems that come with it at scale.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/04/managing-lookup-skew-to-avoid-record-lock-exceptions
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: Get Cloud Consulting needs to integrate two different systems with customer records into the Salesforce Account object. So that no duplicate records are created in Salesforce, Master Data Management will be used. An Architect needs to determine which system is the system of record on a field level. What should the Architect do to achieve this goal?
optionA: Master Data Management systems determine system of record, and the Architect doesn't have to think about what data is controlled by what system.
optionB: Key stakeholders should review any fields that share the same purpose between systems to see how they will be used in Salesforce.
optionC: The database schema for each external system should be reviewed, and fields with different names should always be separate fields in Salesforce.
optionD: Any field that is an input field in either external system will be overwritten by the last record integrated and can never have a system of record.
explanation:
Having key stakeholders review any fields that share the same purpose between systems, to see how they will be used in Salesforce, is what the architect should do. MDM enforces a decision about which system owns a field; it does not make that decision. Two systems whose fields share a purpose have to be compared by the people who know how each is populated and what the field will be used for in Salesforce, and that review is what produces a field-level system of record.
This is a governance-judgment item; Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than the review.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (MDM determines it; the architect need not think about it) — hands the judgment to the tool, which is precisely the step MDM cannot do for you.
Option C (fields with different names are always separate fields) — makes a naming difference into a schema difference, manufacturing duplicate fields for the same concept.
Option D (input fields are overwritten by the last integration and can never have a system of record) — describes last-writer-wins and then declares the problem unsolvable, the ungoverned outcome the whole exercise exists to prevent.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers has a large number of Opportunity fields (100) that they want to track field history on. Which two actions should an architect perform in order to meet this requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create a custom object to store a copy of the record when changed.
optionB: Create a custom object to store the previous and new field values.
optionC: Use Analytic Snapshots to store a copy of the record when changed.
optionD: Select the 100 fields in the Opportunity Set History Tracking page.
explanation:
Creating a custom object to store a copy of the record when changed, and creating a custom object to store the previous and new field values, are the two actions. Standard field history tracking cannot reach 100 fields — "The default limit is 20 fields per object" — and what it does capture is retained for a bounded window rather than indefinitely, so the requirement has to be met by writing the history yourself. A custom object that stores a copy of the record whenever it changes preserves the whole state at each point in time; a custom object that logs the previous and new values for each changed field stores the deltas, which is closer to what field history actually is and far cheaper per change. Either is populated from an Apex trigger.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Analytic Snapshots) — run on a schedule and capture report rows, so they sample state at fixed intervals and miss every change that happens and reverses between two runs.
Option D (select all 100 fields on the Set History Tracking page) — not a configuration anyone can save; the default cap is 20 fields per object.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383595&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_analyticsnapshot.htm

question: Universal Containers has received complaints that customers are being called by multiple Sales Reps where the second Sales Rep that calls is unaware of the previous call by their coworker. What is a data quality problem that could cause this?
optionA: Missing phone number on the Contact record.
optionB: Customer phone number has changed on the Contact record.
optionC: Duplicate Contact records exist in the system.
optionD: Duplicate Activity records on a Contact.
explanation:
Duplicate Contact records existing in the system is the data quality problem. Duplicates split a customer's activity history across multiple records, so a rep working one duplicate cannot see the call logged on the other, producing the uncoordinated duplicate-call symptom.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (missing phone number) — would prevent the call, not cause two uncoordinated ones.
Option B (phone number changed) — would misdirect a call; it would not hide a colleague's logged call.
Option D (duplicate Activity records on one Contact) — both activities sit on the same record, so the second rep would see them.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: (Variant) A data architect is working with a large B2C retailer and needs to model the consumer account structure in Salesforce. What standard feature should be selected in this scenario?
optionA: Individual Accounts
optionB: Account Contact
optionC: Contacts
optionD: Person Accounts
explanation:
Person Accounts are the standard feature to select. A person account "stores information about individual consumers" — one record that carries both account and contact attributes, which is what a B2C model needs when there is no employing organisation to hang a Contact from.
Before enabling this in a real org, read Considerations for Using Person Accounts — the feature changes Account behaviour org-wide and cannot be turned off.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Individual Accounts) — not a Salesforce feature; the standard object named Individual exists, but it holds data privacy and consent preferences, not the consumer's account record.
Option B (Account Contact) — an account-and-contact pair still requires a parent Account, and inventing one shared parent for consumers produces the parent-child data skew Salesforce warns against.
Option C (Contacts) — a Contact alone needs a parent Account for the same reason.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.account_person_behavior.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) requires 2 years of customer related cases to be available on SF for operational reporting. Any cases older than 2 years and upto 7 years need to be available on demand to the Service agents. UC creates 5 million cases per yr. Which 2 data archiving strategies should a data architect recommend? Choose 2 options.
optionA: Use custom objects for cases older than 2 years and use nightly batch to move them.
optionB: Sync cases older than 2 years to an external database, and provide access to Service agents to the database
optionC: Use big objects for cases older than 2 years, and use nightly batch to move them.
optionD: Use Heroku and external objects to display cases older than 2 years and bulk API to hard delete from Salesforce.
explanation:
Big objects for cases older than two years moved by nightly batch, and Heroku with external objects to display them plus Bulk API hard delete from Salesforce, are the two strategies. Big objects hold the 2-to-7-year archive on-platform at scale without storage or performance penalties; Heroku with external objects surfaces archived cases on demand inside Salesforce, and the Bulk API hard delete reclaims storage from the transactional store.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom objects for old cases, nightly batch) — a standard custom object still consumes storage and degrades at 25 million-plus rows; the problem is moved, not solved.
Option B (sync to an external database, give agents database access) — exporting to a raw external database without virtualisation makes on-demand access from inside Salesforce harder for agents, not easier.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bigobjects.meta/bigobjects/big_object.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_techniques_deleting_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: A large insurance provider is looking to implement Salesforce. The following exist. 1. Multiple channel for lead acquisition 2. Duplication leads across channels 3. Poor customer experience and higher costs On analysis, it found that there are duplicate leads that are resulting to mitigate the issues?
optionA: Build process is manually search and merge duplicates.
optionB: Standardize lead information across all channels.
optionC: Build a custom solution to identify and merge duplicate leads.
optionD: Implement a third-party solution to clean and enrich lead data.
optionE: Implement de-duplication strategy to prevent duplicate leads
explanation:
Standardising lead information across all channels, implementing a third-party solution to clean and enrich lead data, and implementing a de-duplication strategy are the three actions. Standardising capture formats and fields across channels reduces the inconsistencies that create near-duplicates, a third-party cleanse and enrich service validates and corrects lead data at scale, and a de-duplication strategy using native matching and duplicate rules prevents duplicates at entry.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (manual search and merge) — costly, slow, and it never stops the next duplicate arriving.
Option C (a custom solution to identify and merge duplicates) — a bespoke build of what duplicate rules already do, and hard to maintain.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Developers at Universal Containers need to build a report for the business which displays Accounts opened in the past year grouped by industry. This report will also include information from contacts, opportunities, and orders. There are several million Accounts in the system. Which two options should be recommended to make this report perform well and satisfy the business need?
optionA: Use triggers to populate denormalized related fields on the Account.
optionB: Use formula fields to surface information from related entities on the report.
optionC: Use unbounded date ranges to filter the report.
optionD: Use an indexed date field with bounded date filters.
explanation:
Triggers that populate denormalised related fields on the Account, and an indexed date field with bounded date filters, are the two recommendations. The LDV guide's reporting advice is to cut both joins and rows. Denormalising the related data onto the Account with triggers is its "De-normalize data when practical… Use summarized data stored on the parent record for the report" — the report then reads one object instead of joining Contact, Opportunity and Order across several million Accounts. An indexed date field with a bounded filter is the other half: "Use report filters that emphasize the use of standard or custom indexed fields", and a bounded range is what lets the optimizer use that index.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (cross-object formula fields) — evaluated at query time on every row, so they add the join cost back that denormalising removed.
Option C (unbounded date ranges) — defeat index selectivity outright and send the query to a full scan.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_reporting.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: Universal Containers is exporting 40 million Account records from Salesforce using Informatica Cloud. The ETL tool fails and the query log indicates a full table scan time-out failure. What is the recommended solution?
optionA: Modify the export job header to specify Export-in-Parallel.
optionB: Modify the export query with LIMIT clause with Batch size 10,000.
optionC: Modify the export query that includes standard index fields(s).
optionD: Modify the export job header to specify Sforce-Enable-PKChunking.
explanation:
Modifying the export job header to specify Sforce-Enable-PKChunking is the recommended solution. PK Chunking splits the 40-million-row extract into ID-range batches the Bulk API processes independently, so no single query has to scan the whole table — which is what was timing out.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Export-in-Parallel header) — no such header exists; parallelism does not shorten a full-table scan anyway.
Option B (LIMIT with a batch size of 10,000) — LIMIT truncates the result; it does not page through the table, and each query still starts with the same unselective scan.
Option C (include standard indexed fields in the query) — can help selectivity for a filtered extract, but does not address extracting the entire table.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/async_api_headers_enable_pk_chunking.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has recently implemented Salesforce to track opportunities across all their regions. NTO sales teams across all regions have historically managed their sales process in Microsoft Excel. NTO sales teams are complaining that their data from the Excel files were not migrated as part of the implementation and NTO is now facing low Salesforce adoption. What should a data architect recommend to increase Salesforce adoption?
optionA: Use the Excel connector to Salesforce to sync data from individual Excel files.
optionB: Define a standard mapping and train sales users to import opportunity data.
optionC: Load data in external database and provide access to database to sales users.
optionD: Create a chatter group and upload all Excel files to the group.
explanation:
Defining a standard mapping and training sales users to import their opportunity data is the recommendation. The adoption problem is that the reps' actual working data never arrived; a standard field mapping from the spreadsheets to Opportunity, plus training, puts that history into Salesforce and, just as importantly, leaves the reps able to do it again without filing a ticket.
This is a change-adoption judgment item rather than a documented rule.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Excel connector syncing individual files) — keeps the spreadsheets authoritative, which is the habit the implementation was meant to end.
Option C (an external database with access for sales users) — adds a system nobody asked for and keeps the data out of Salesforce.
Option D (upload the Excel files to a Chatter group) — stores them as attachments: not reportable, not forecastable, and no better than the shared drive they came from.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.admin_exportdata.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: UC is using SF CRM. UC sales managers are complaining about data quality and would like to monitor and measure data quality. Which 2 solutions should a data architect recommend to monitor and measure data quality? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use custom objects and fields to identify issues.
optionB: Review data quality reports and dashboards.
optionC: Install and run data quality analysis dashboard app
optionD: Export data and check for data completeness outside of Salesforce.
explanation:
Reviewing data quality reports and dashboards, and installing the data quality analysis dashboard app, are the two solutions. Monitoring means something that keeps producing numbers without anyone remembering to run it: reports and dashboards built on the quality dimensions the org cares about do that natively, and the Data Quality Analysis Dashboards app from Salesforce Labs packages the same idea — formula fields that score completeness on Leads, Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities and more, surfaced as dashboards — free, and installable without building it yourself.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom objects and fields to identify issues) — a build with no measurement attached.
Option D (export and check completeness outside Salesforce) — a one-off audit that tells the sales managers nothing next month.
References:
https://appexchange.salesforce.com/appxListingDetail?listingId=a0N300000016cshEAA
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is streaming IoT data from connected devices to a cloud database. Every 24 hours. 100,000 records are generated. NTO employees will need to see these records within Salesforce and generate weekly reports on it. Developers may also need to write programmatic logic to aggregate the records and incorporate them into workflows. Which data pattern will allow a data architect to satisfy these requirements, while also keeping limits in mind?
optionA: Bidirectional integration
optionB: Unidirectional integration
optionC: Virtualization
optionD: Persistence
explanation:
Persistence — storing the IoT records in Salesforce objects — is the pattern. The third requirement forces it: developers need to aggregate the records in Apex and feed them into workflows, and external objects do not support Apex triggers and have a narrow automation surface, so virtualised data cannot carry that logic. Weekly reporting on persisted records is straightforward once they are objects. At 100,000 records a day, load them with the Bulk API to keep API consumption in hand.
That is an exception to Salesforce's default advice, which runs the other way: "Unless the data absolutely needs to reside in Salesforce, consider data virtualization with Salesforce Connect instead", because "More data in your organization ultimately leads to larger data volumes, which can adversely affect performance and add technical debt."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (bidirectional integration) — describes which way data flows, not whether it is stored; a different question from the one asked.
Option B (unidirectional integration) — the same.
Option C (virtualization) — would satisfy the reporting requirement on its own; it is the programmatic aggregation and workflow participation that rule it out here.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_external_objects_considerations.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_external_objects.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is concerned that data is being corrupted daily either through negligence or maliciousness. They want to implement a backup strategy to help recover any corrupted data or data mistakenly changed or even deleted. What should the data architect consider when designing a field-level audit and recovery plan?
optionA: Reduce data storage by purging old data.
optionB: Implement an AppExchange package.
optionC: Review projected data storage needs.
optionD: Schedule a weekly export file.
explanation:
Reviewing projected data storage needs is the consideration the plan turns on. Field-level audit and recovery means keeping the old values, not just the current ones, and keeping them long enough to recover from something noticed weeks later; that is a storage question before it is a tooling one.
Be aware the item is loose.
