Option B, an AppExchange backup package, is how most orgs actually get granular field-level recovery, and it answers "what should the architect consider" nearly as directly as C does. C is keyed because it names a planning input rather than a product, but the two are not cleanly separated by the stem.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (purge old data to reduce storage) — the opposite of what a recovery plan needs.
Option B (an AppExchange package) — a legitimate route to field-level recovery and the item's weak point; not keyed because the exam wants the planning input, not the product.
Option D (a weekly export) — a seven-day blast radius and no field-level granularity; it restores a record as it was last Saturday, not the one field somebody corrupted on Wednesday.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383595&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.admin_exportdata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Item defect: distractor B (an AppExchange backup package) is a reasonable answer to "what should the architect consider" for granular field-level recovery, and nothing in the stem separates a planning input from a tooling choice.

question: A national nonprofit organization is using Salesforce to recruit members. The recruitment process requires a member to be matched with a volunteer opportunity. Given the following: 1. A record is created in Project__c and used to track the project through completion. 2. The member may then start volunteering and is required to track their volunteer hours, which is stored in VTOTime__c object related to the project. 3. Ability to view or edit the VTOTime__c object needs to be the same as the Project__c record. 4. Managers must see total hours volunteered while viewing the Project__c record. Which data relationship should the data architect use to support this requirement when creating the custom VTOTime__c object?
optionA: Lookup Field on Project__c to VTOTime__c displaying a list of VTOTime__c in a related list.
optionB: Lookup field on VTOTime__c to Project__c with formula field on Project__c showing Sum of hours from VTOTime__c records.
optionC: Master-Detail Field on VTOTime__c to Project__c with roll-up summary field on Project__c showing sum of hours from VTOTime__c records.
optionD: Master-Detail field on Project__c to VTOTime__c showing a list of VTOTime__c Records in a related list.
explanation:
A Master-Detail field on VTOTime__c to Project__c, with a roll-up summary field on Project__c summing the hours, is the relationship. Two of the four requirements pick it between them: access parity — VTOTime__c must be viewable and editable exactly as its Project__c is — comes free with master-detail, because detail records "inherit the master's sharing and security settings"; and total hours on the Project record needs a roll-up summary, which requires a master-detail relationship.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (lookup on Project__c to VTOTime__c) — the relationship field belongs on the child, and a lookup gives neither inherited access nor roll-ups.
Option B (lookup on VTOTime__c with a formula on Project__c) — a formula field evaluates against its own record; it cannot sum values across child records, which is precisely the job roll-up summary exists for. And a lookup does not inherit sharing.
Option D (master-detail on Project__c to VTOTime__c) — backwards: the master-detail field lives on the detail object, so it belongs on VTOTime__c pointing at Project__c.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/relationships_among_objects.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Which two statements are accurate with respect to performance testing a Force.com application?
optionA: All Force.com applications must be performance tested in a sandbox as well as production.
optionB: A performance test plan must be created and submitted to Salesforce customer support.
optionC: Applications with highly customized code or large volumes should be performance tested.
optionD: Application performance benchmarked in a sandbox can also be expected in production.
explanation:
A performance test plan must be submitted to Salesforce customer support, and applications with highly customised code or large volumes should be performance tested — those are the two accurate statements. Salesforce requires approval before you load-test the platform, and the requirement is concrete: "Submit an LAP request for approval at least one week before the testing date", with a test plan document, dates, sandbox org id, business scenario and justification. "All tests must be pre-approved. Unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking." And the applications worth putting through this are the ones whose behaviour is not already known — heavy custom code, or large data volumes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (must be tested in a sandbox and in production) — describes something Salesforce forbids: "Because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox for testing", and "scale tests are only permitted in sandboxes."
Option D (sandbox benchmarks can be expected in production) — fails for the reason a full copy sandbox is specified in the first place: a sandbox with different data volumes is not a predictor of production.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2020/09/introduction-to-performance-testing

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option A with "not all apps must be tested in both environments", which leaves a learner believing production performance testing is sometimes required. Salesforce does not permit performance testing in production at all — it is sandbox-only, and every test needs prior approval.

question: Universal Containers would like to remove data silos and connect their legacy CRM together with their ERP and with Salesforce. Most of their sales team has already migrated to Salesforce for daily use, although a few users are still on the old CRM until some functionality they require is completed. Which two techniques should be used for smooth interoperability now and in the future.
optionA: Replicate ongoing changes in the legacy CRM to Salesforce to facilitate a smooth transition when the legacy CRM is eventually retired.
optionB: Specify the legacy CRM as the system of record during transition until it is removed from operation and fully replaced by Salesforce.
optionC: Work with stakeholders to establish a Master Data Management plan for the system of record for specific objects, records, and fields.
optionD: Do not connect Salesforce and the legacy CRM to each other during this transition period, but do allow both to interact with the ERP.
explanation:
Specifying the legacy CRM as the system of record during the transition, and working with stakeholders on an MDM plan for the system of record per object, record and field, are the two techniques. Two systems are live and both can write, so the first thing to settle is who is right today: naming the legacy CRM the system of record for the transition period removes the ambiguity while the remaining users are still on it. The second is who will be right tomorrow, per object and per field, as functionality moves across — that is what an MDM plan agreed with stakeholders gives you, and it is the part that survives the legacy system's retirement.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than ranking these choices.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (replicate legacy changes into Salesforce) — a mechanism you might well implement, but it presumes the authority question is already answered.
Option D (do not connect the two CRMs, let both talk to the ERP) — a routing rule, not a governance decision; it leaves the ERP mediating conflicts nobody has adjudicated.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a Service Cloud call center application and has a multi system support solution. UC would like or ensure that all systems have access to the same customer information. What solution should a data architect recommend?
optionA: Make Salesforce the system of record for all data.
optionB: Implement a master data management (MDM) strategy for customer data.
optionC: Load customer data in all systems.
optionD: Let each system be an owner of data it generates.
explanation:
Implementing a master data management strategy for customer data is the recommendation. "All systems have access to the same customer information" is a consistency requirement, and consistency needs an arbiter: an MDM strategy supplies a golden customer record with survivorship rules deciding which system's value wins for each attribute, which every system then reads.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce as system of record for all data) — a decision made before looking at which system is actually authoritative for which data.
Option C (load customer data into every system) — creates the copies that drift.
Option D (each system owns the data it generates) — reasonable-sounding, and it reproduces exactly the silos the stem complains about: the customer's address exists in three places and no rule says which one is current.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://architect.salesforce.com/decision-guides/data-integration

question: NTO (Northern Trail Outlets) has a complex Salesforce org which has been developed over past 5 years. Internal users are complaining abt multiple data issues, including incomplete and duplicate data in the org. NTO has decided to engage a data architect to analyze and define data quality standards. Which 3 key factors should a data architect consider while defining data quality standards? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Define data duplication standards and rules
optionB: Define key fields in staging database for data cleansing
optionC: Measure data timeliness and consistency
optionD: Finalize an extract transform load (ETL) tool for data migration
explanation:
Defining data duplication standards and rules, measuring data timeliness and consistency, and measuring data completeness and accuracy are the three factors. Defining quality standards means naming the dimensions you will hold the data to and how each is measured: duplication standards and matching rules define what counts as the same record; timeliness and consistency cover how current a value must be and whether the same fact is recorded the same way everywhere; completeness and accuracy cover whether required information is present and correct — the two complaints the stem actually names.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (key fields in a staging database for cleansing) — a migration decision about how data moves, not a statement of what "good" means.
Option D (finalise an ETL tool) — a tooling decision that would not appear in a standards document.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/well-architected/trusted/compliant
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_duplicaterule.htm

question: (Variant) NTO has decided that it is going to build a channel sales portal with the following requirements: 1. External resellers are able to authenticate to the portal with a login. 2. Lead data, opportunity data and order data are available to authenticated users. 3. Authenticated users many need to run reports and dashboards. 4. There is no need for more than 10 custom objects or additional file storage. Which community cloud license type should a data architect recommend to meet the portal requirements?
optionA: Customer community.
optionB: Lightning external apps starter.
optionC: Customer community plus.
optionD: Partner community.
explanation:
Partner Community is the licence type. Leads, opportunities and orders are sales objects, and the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries them along with reports and dashboards in the site — the combination a channel sales portal for resellers needs. The stem's fourth requirement — no more than 10 custom objects and no extra file storage — is there to tell you the cheaper external licences are not being ruled out by object count, so the sales objects and reporting are what decide it.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Customer Community) — built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and does not extend to leads and opportunities.
Option B (Lightning External Apps Starter) — sized for custom apps rather than CRM sales objects with reporting.
Option C (Customer Community Plus) — adds reports, dashboards and role-based sharing to Customer Community, but still no leads or opportunities.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_understanding_license_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: DreamHouse Realty has an integration that creates records in a Salesforce Custom Object. The Custom Object has a field marked as required on the page layout. DreamHouse Realty has noticed that many of the records coming from the external system are missing data in this field. The Architect needs to ensure this field always contains data coming from the source system. Which two approaches should the Architect take? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Set up a Validation Rule to prevent blank values.
optionB: Create a Workflow to default a value into this field.
optionC: Mark the field required in setup at the field level.
optionD: Blame the customer's external system for bad data.
explanation:
A validation rule to prevent blank values, and marking the field required at the field level in Setup, are the two approaches. Required on a page layout is a UI rule: it applies to the users looking at that layout and to nothing else, so an integration writing through the API sails past it. Both keyed options work at a level the API cannot bypass. A universally required field "must have a value whenever a record is saved within Salesforce, the Lightning Platform API, Connect Offline, Salesforce for Outlook, the Self-Service portal, or automated processes", and a validation rule rejecting blank values runs on every save path too, and gives a message naming the problem.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a workflow to default a value) — makes the records look complete while losing the fact that the source system sent nothing; the opposite of ensuring the data comes from the source.
Option D (blame the external system) — not an approach.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_universally_required_field_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm
